articles.title_orig: China Finds Another Route to Protein -This Time From Industrial Gas
articles.title_zh: China Finds Another Route to Protein -This Time From Industrial Gas
articles.content_orig:
China's search for new ways to produce protein is taking another interesting turn. Researchers at the Tianjin Institute of Industrial Biotechnology are investigating how industrial gases can be converted into nutrients for microorganisms capable of producing protein. It's another indication China isn't betting on a single technology to strengthen its future food supply.
The process begins with syngas — a mixture of gases that can be generated from industrial processes or biomass. Through fermentation, microorganisms convert these gases into compounds including acetate, which can then feed a second fermentation process. Chinese researchers have been testing how this nutrient-rich liquid can support the growth of Yarrowia lipolytica , a yeast with potential applications in microbial protein production.
The early results are encouraging. Researchers reported a 7.7% improvement in yeast biomass production in a five-litre fermenter, alongside an increase in acetate conversion from 21.68% to 41.1%. These are laboratory-scale results, not evidence that commercially competitive food protein is about to reach supermarket shelves. Nevertheless, they demonstrate another possible route towards producing useful biomass without relying exclusively on conventional crops or livestock.
What makes this particularly interesting is the wider Chinese strategy. From precision fermentation and cultivated proteins to microbial biomass and alternative fermentation feedstocks, Chinese researchers are exploring multiple approaches to protein production. Each has different technical and economic challenges, but collectively they could expand the country's future production options.
For countries such as New Zealand, the question is worth asking: if protein can increasingly be produced using industrial carbon streams, microorganisms and controlled fermentation systems, how might that change the economics of food production and national food security? China appears determined to find out.

articles.title_orig: San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing
articles.title_zh: San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing
articles.content_orig:
Lauren Goldboss is busy. The owner of a small San Francisco dog-walking company, she has been hiring staff and buying vans.
Fuelling the growth is her new office dog-walking service Paw Perk, popular with some local AI start-ups.
Her business is an example of how the AI boom in San Francisco is benefiting other sectors.
The city saw an exodus of residents during the pandemic and its downtown was weakened by remote work, but it s now enjoying a rejuvenation, with AI being the major driver.
Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic – which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries – are based here. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, last week listed on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.
Thousands of other AI start-ups have also sprung up in San Francisco.
Signs of the boom are evident in soaring rents and house prices, falling office vacancies, and buses and billboards plastered with cryptic AI adverts.
But what if there is a significant downward correction in AI share prices and a resulting big fall in investment in the industry? The International Monetary Fund last month became the latest organization to warn that this was a possibility.
Concerns have since continued due to the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, the former boss of AI firm Nvidia, based south of San Francisco, causing some wider AI stock falls. However, Nvidia remains highly profitable, and Wednesday of this week it reported that its latest quarterly profits had doubled from a year earlier to $65bn (£49bn).
What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco – no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles – be preparing for a possible crash?
One AI worker, employed by one of the largest companies in the city, is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come down… and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name.
He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China.
But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?"
Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, says that a significant market correction is "totally possible".
Yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he says that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity.
"In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great."
If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south.
That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley.
One study found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley.
But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear.
For all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn.
"Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new company formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank.
Ted Egan, the chief economist for the City and County of San Francisco, adds that "because of AI, it is a good time for tech again in the city, but we are not seeing tonnes of overall tech job growth".
Despite the expansion of the AI sector, the city remains about 35,000 jobs shy of its pre-pandemic peak, estimates Enrico Moretti, an economics professor at the University of California, Berkeley.
Instead, much of the spending by AI firms in the US is going towards data centres and computing power, relatively little of which are located in the Bay Area. San Francisco might be the brains of the AI boom, but it isn't the brawn.
Nonetheless, a significant correction could still be "very painful" for San Francisco, warns Moretti. Less AI hiring and potential layoffs would ripple through the local service sector, likely to affect jobs in everything from restaurants, to retail, to personal services like dog walking.
"It is the spillover on service jobs that would actually be the main effect," he says.
Office vacancies could also rise, reducing downtown foot traffic, while rents and house prices could weaken.
But AI isn't the only force driving San Francisco's recovery. Healthcare and tourism – which the city has been working to encourage, including by improving downtown safety and cleanliness – are also growing, which may help cushion against a possible AI downturn.
"Tourism is not fully back, but the growth has been healthy," says Egan, adding that it is a sign of confidence in San Francisco.
All told, Egan doesn't expect an AI crash to fundamentally alter San Francisco's economic trajectory.
"The city's economy has not been screaming during this AI boom, so I wouldn't expect it to grind to a halt if there was a slowdown in AI spending," he says. "I think of it primarily as a hiccup that we should expect, rather than a major course correction for the city's economy."
As to whether and how San Francisco's city government should prepare, there are limits to what it can do, note Bellisario and Moretti. But encouraging growth in sectors beyond technology and maintaining financial reserves could help.
For Goldboss, the dog-walking company owner, her philosophy is to "build while it is here". If the next tech bust comes – "always a reality in San Francisco" – she will try to adapt to what the market needs. "It is just the risk you kind of have to take," she says.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Tracked Alice Huang’s Contacts With China Spy Agency During Nvidia Affair
articles.title_zh: U.S. Tracked Alice Huang’s Contacts With China Spy Agency During Nvidia Affair
articles.content_orig:
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with China's President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit on Nov. 19, 2026.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is placing particular focus on renewing relations with China as he aims to deepen international trade ties and diversify from U.S. reliance amid a three-month-long trade war with the U.S.
When asked what cards Canada holds in its ongoing talks with Washington, Carney, who recently announced a new partnership with the E.U. , pointed to the country's budding relationships elsewhere.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said Wednesday during a remote interview with the New York Times from Shenzhen, China, where he was among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit . "If the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy.” His remarks came in the wake of President Donald Trump's claim that the U.S. holds “all the cards” after trade talks collapsed in August, leading to both sides enforcing heavy retaliatory tariffs .
Carney and Trump had a meeting on the sidelines of APEC, but aside from a commitment to “continue” negotiations and stay in close contact, no progress was made. However, Carney painted his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a much more positive light. Ahead of the summit, Carney and Xi announced a Canada-China trade pact , which provided additional tariff relief on Canadian food and agricultural exports into China, and in return saw Canada agree to extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
Carney, who is promoting a “Canada Strong” platform as he aims to build economic resilience at home, touted the expansion of the trade arrangement with China as something that will deliver “greater certainty and prosperity for all Canadians.” He also praised the negotiation process with China, saying: “They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”
In an eight-day tour that took him from a European summit in Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia, and finally China for the APEC gathering, Carney forged ahead with his plan to diversify Canada's economy away from its dependence on the U.S., which by far remains the country's largest trading partner .
Experts say Canada's progress in deepening its economic relationships with China could challenge Trump's insistence that Washington holds the upper hand in trade negotiations.
“Part of the Trump Administration’s [belief] is that everybody needs the U.S. more than anything else, and therefore the U.S. has maximum leverage,” says Jennifer Hillman, co-director of the Institute of International Economic Law at Georgetown University. “What this is clearly saying is that Canada can afford to be less willing to give the U.S. whatever it asks for [in negotiations], because they have other options.”
China has the world's second-largest economy , behind only the U.S., giving it the potential to become a much larger market for Canadian goods than some of the other countries Carney has sought to deepen relations with.
“China represents a very big market and the potential of a really big trading partner,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University, noting it could be a leverage point in U.S. negotiations. “Doing a deal with a country like China is something that [the U.S.] will care about because of the size of China's economy and its competitive relationship with the U.S.”
Carney's latest push to strengthen trade ties with Beijing forms part of a months-long effort to renew Canada-China relations. In January, he met with Xi to forge what he called a “ new strategic partnership ,” agreeing to allow in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff of 6.1%, rather than the previous 100% levy. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
The move drew criticism from Trump, who said that “China will eat Canada alive, completely devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life.”
While Canada's closer relationship with China could strengthen its hand in negotiations, experts also warn that it could backfire.
Turnbull points to the latest agreement to extend tariff exemptions on Chinese steel and aluminum as a potential source of tension with Washington. “Things like reducing tariffs on select steel and aluminum products coming from China is something that might make the U.S. and not just Donald Trump, but also [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer angry,” she suggests.
Steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs were among the major points of contention when U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down in August, with both sides accusing each other of walking back commitments.
Carney, however, has played down concerns that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is a major issue for Trump.
“In my conversation with the President, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Meanwhile, some Canadian officials have voiced concerns on expanding trade with China.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned Carney on Monday against opening the door for more Chinese-made EV vehicles in Canada, arguing the “government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars.”
Michael Chong, a lawmaker from Canada’s Conservative Party, during a press conference on Wednesday supported maintaining a dialogue with Beijing, but described Carney’s budding strategic partnership with China as a “risky gambit,” citing potential “national security” concerns.
In 2025, Ottawa identified China as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage against Canada alongside other countries such as Russia and Iran. The Canadian government’s own analysis of Canada-China relations also points out that there are "associated risks” in broader trade cooperation in key areas, such as “prevalent and persistent intellectual property theft, and the risk of diversion of sensitive goods and technologies intended for civilian use for military purposes and applications.”
Carney said ahead of his Asia trip that he would raise concerns about foreign interference in his meeting with Xi. "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” he told reporters in Montreal on Nov. 10. Carney added that he would stress the importance Canada places on "the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”
In a press briefing during the APEC summit, Carney emphasized that Canada's trade with China is largely focused on commodities, rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
“We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork. We are exporting halibut,” Carney said , also citing liquefied natural gas and oil. “These are important industries. These are not cutting-edge semi-conductors.”
Experts point out that Canada could pursue deeper cooperation with other international partners in sectors where a closer relationship with China would be more difficult, including defense and advanced technology.
“[Canada] is not going to partner with China on defense, security, AI, and digital technology, things like that would be very difficult. [Carney] would have an impossible time trying to convince Canadians that's what we should be doing,” says Turnbull. “For those things, [Canada] would be putting [its] arms around the European Union.”

The southern city of Odesa and surrounding areas have suffered "serious damage" to their main power grids following repeated Russian attacks on critical infrastructure, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo said on Nov. 22.
The electricity supply situation in Odesa Oblast is "extremely difficult" after key power infrastructure supplying households sustained "significant" damage. Repair crews are working to restore electricity, but continued Russian attacks and air raid alerts are disrupting their work, according to Ukrenergo.
"The situation is significantly complicated by constant threats of new attacks and air raid alerts, which prevent repair crews from always working continuously," the company said .
The situation in the Odesa area worsened following the large-scale Russian attack on Nov. 20, after which regional governor Oleh Kiper reported disruptions to the power grids.
The outages have disrupted daily life across the city. Schools in Odesa will switch to online classes for a week starting Nov. 23, local authorities said .
The power cuts have also forced the city to temporarily suspend electric public transportation, including trolleybuses. Local media have also reported disruptions to water and heating supplies.
The damage in Odesa comes as Russia intensifies its attacks on Ukrainian critical infrastructure across the country in recent months, targeting power grids, substations, and water supply facilities as the temperature continues to drop.
Ukraine faces an increasingly severe shortage of Patriot interceptor missiles that can counter ballistic threats, making it difficult for the country to defend itself from the intensifying attacks.
The power and water supply situation across Ukraine, including in Kyiv, has significantly worsened over November, with Russia launching its latest massive aerial assault with missiles and drones on Nov. 20.
The Energy Ministry said on Nov. 22 that Russia attacked an unspecified number of energy facilities over the past day, leaving households in central-eastern Dnipropetrovsk, western Zhytomyr, northeastern Kharkiv, and Odesa oblasts without power this morning.
Of these regions, Odesa Oblast faces the most difficult situation, the ministry said.
"The enemy is purposefully attacking energy facilities important for the region's power supply," the ministry said . "As a result, a significant number of consumers remain without power," it added, without elaborating on the number.
The utility workers managed to partially restore power to critical infrastructure facilities in the Odesa area this morning, and backup power schemes are currently being developed to restore electricity to the rest, according to Ukrenergo.

I had an interesting question yesterday that I would like to address. I will paraphrase, but essentially, the person wanted to know why technicians (and while he used that term, I believe, since he was speaking to me, he meant ME!) feel they need to line up all the indicators when (according to this person) we often never get the perfect setup for a rally.
For me, it is because for the forty-plus years I have been doing this, I have been a slave to my indicators. If they line up, then I am good to go with what they say. Can my own interpretation be incorrect? Of course. No one gets it right all the time. But I like to play the odds, and for me the odds say if I wait for the indicators to line up, my odds are better.
I don’t know why he thinks we often never get the perfect setup. My indicators were plenty bullish in late March, and they were bullish on the SOX again in late July. I would also point out that those same indicators were not bullish on the broadening-out story that was widespread in early August.
As for this point in time, I have been talking about sentiment being complacent for months on end. In the last two weeks, we have finally seen that change. I would say most of those sentiment indicators are not extreme, but they show a much different bias than we had even a week ago.
The Investors Intelligence bulls are still at 41%, and the bears are too low at 24%. AAII is similar: I don’t see an extreme there. The National Association of Active Investment Managers (NAAIM) who were on margin in September have really pulled in their horns as their exposure now sits at 51. That is lower than the spring, although not quite as low as the Tariff Tantrum. So, no, it’s not extreme, but it is a giant shift.
The ten-day moving average of the put/call ratio is finally closing in on the reading we saw in late July.  I have been waiting for months for this to lift, and it finally has.
The DSI for the S&P is now at 10, and Nasdaq is also at 10. The last time these got this low was early April 2025, during the Tariff Tantrum. Before that was late September/early October 2022. I want to remind you that the DSI for bonds got to single digits in September, but bonds still had one last fling down (rates up) before it mattered.
So here is a chart of 2022. I’m using this because I have used 2022 before with you (another bear market period). The arrow shows the time when the DSI got to 9 for both the S&P and Nasdaq. The rally didn’t last, but we did get a rally, six percent in a few days.
My indicators are set up to get short-term oversold midweek next week. I think we get an oversold rally. I also think you shouldn’t get married to it. You trade it.

articles.title_orig: Delta computer outage disrupts flights at MSP ahead of Thanksgiving
articles.title_zh: Delta computer outage disrupts flights at MSP ahead of Thanksgiving
articles.content_orig:
Delta Air Lines has resolved an issue with its weight and balance system that caused nationwide delays leading into a busy Thanksgiving travel week, the airline said.
Calculating weight and balance on an aircraft is a critical part of the pre-departure preparations. Delta was forced to use “manual workarounds” on Sunday morning “to safely get flights departed,” the airline told CNN affiliate WSB-TV , as delays rippled across its network.
The system’s automation for departing flight weight and balance calculations is now working, Delta said. But passengers could still experience lingering effects from the holdup.
Over half of Delta’s total flights were delayed and 4% were canceled as of 7:30 p.m. ET on Sunday, according to flight tracking website FlightAware. Delta has said about 70% of Sunday’s schedule changes were due to the automation issue, which caused an hourslong ground delay at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport – Delta’s biggest travel hub and the busiest airport in the world .
The ground delay was canceled around 11:30 a.m. ET, according to an FAA advisory .
“Delta teams are focused on completing the remainder of today’s schedule. Cancellations, as always, are a last resort when all other options have been exhausted,” Delta told CNN, apologizing to customers for the delay in their travels.
Calculating weight and balance on an aircraft ensures the fully loaded aircraft is not too heavy to fly, is loaded properly and the pilots have the right settings for a safe takeoff.
Major airlines use sophisticated computer programs at their headquarters to calculate these numbers.
“Compliance with the weight and balance limits of any aircraft is critical to flight safety,” according to the FAA’s Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge .
For Delta, the weight and balance instructions for baggage crews are planned at the Operations and Customer Center in the Atlanta headquarters using a system called ALIS, or Automated Load Instruction System.
“Right now, it’s a system-wide outage for Delta Air Lines,” an employee explained to a pilot in Boston on Sunday morning in a radio call captured by ATC.com . “The ramp isn’t really able to load because there is no ramp worksheet in there, so that’s what we’re doing, we’re manually counting bags and doing a report for you guys.”
“Oh, geez,” the pilot responded.
“Kinda like the good old days across here,” the ramp worker noted sarcastically.
The Delta slowdowns come at the outset of what is projected to be a busy holiday travel period. Over four million travelers are expected at Delta’s Atlanta hub between November 19 and December 1, according to a news release from the airport.
Many travelers have already experienced long lines and frustrating disruptions in recent weeks after all flights nationwide were grounded just over a week ago, sparking flight delays and cancellations for several days.
The FAA has said the outages that triggered the nationwide ground stop likely stemmed from an outdated copper wire at a remote location.
Sunday’s Delta delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems, the FAA confirmed in a social media post .
The ground delay affected Delta flights and was not airport-wide, a spokesperson for Hartsfield-Jackson told CNN in a statement.
More than 60% of flights out of Hartsfield-Jackson were delayed Sunday evening, according to FlightAware, while around half of inbound flights to the airport were also delayed. The data does not specify how many of these delays were Delta flights.
Atlanta resident Shane Rocha and her family were traveling through Hartsfield-Jackson on Sunday morning to visit family, Rocha told CNN affiliate WANF. Rocha said she had flown earlier in the week without any issues and was hoping that today’s travel would be equally smooth.
“Luckily we’re only 19 minutes delayed, knock on wood,” she said. “Hopefully it stays that low.”
Although the specifics surrounding the Delta issue remain unclear, United Airlines experienced an issue with its weight and balance computer system in 2025 that triggered more than 1,000 delays and dozens of cancellations, the airline said at the time.
United also experienced a brief system outage on November 16 that affected fewer than 150 flights across the US, the airline told CNN. This outage appears unrelated to Sunday’s Delta automation issue and the previous nationwide FAA ground stop.
At the time of United’s outage, the FAA said the incident was not an agency equipment issue and the airline said there is no indication it was cybersecurity-related.
Beyond system disruptions, severe weather in the Northeastern United States has caused headaches as many people travel for the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday.
Passengers flying to New York’s LaGuardia Airport and New Jersey’s Newark Liberty International Airport can expect around two hours of weather-related ground delays on average, according to FAA updates .
Weather has also sparked delays for flights to San Francisco, while San Diego and several Florida airports are experiencing departure hold-ups due to a high volume of flights.

articles.title_orig: China's industrial strength benefits global growth
articles.title_zh: China's industrial strength benefits global growth
articles.content_orig:
By MA SI in Shenzhen, Guangdong | 
          China Daily |
          Updated: 2026-11-23 07:26
China's manufacturing prowess is not "stealing jobs" from the rest of the world but creating shared opportunities through localized production, technology transfers and complementary trade, business leaders and experts said.
They made the comments during the 2026 APEC Economic Leaders' Week in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, pushing back against the so-called "China Shock 2.0" narrative that portrays the country's industrial rise as a zero-sum threat to global employment.
Wang Chuanfu, chairman and president of Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD, said many people outside China have some misconceptions about the country's manufacturing capabilities.
Citing BYD's operations in Chile, Wang said the company purchases large quantities of copper and lithium there and supplies Chinese electric buses that help improve the local environment.
"Our trade is complementary," he said. "We not only export Chinese technology to the world but also bring jobs and tax revenue to local communities, achieving mutually beneficial cooperation and win-win outcomes."
He said that the company's plant in Thailand, with an annual production capacity of 150,000 new energy vehicles, employs nearly 6,000 workers, more than 95 percent of them Thai. He added that most components are sourced locally. Similar arrangements exist at BYD's plants in Indonesia and Brazil.
"We work with 12,000 suppliers globally and aim to benefit the world with Chinese technology through local procurement and research and development," Wang said.
Lei Jun, CEO and chairman of Xiaomi, said, "Asia-Pacific economies form the world's core industrial and supply chain region and the most promising consumer market with strong complementarity and cooperation potential despite their differences."
The company's cars and smartphones require thousands of components, which can only be completed through global supply chain collaboration, he said. "Xiaomi cars will officially enter overseas markets next year," Lei added.
Noting that the automotive industry is a pillar industry in many countries, Lei said cooperating with local supply chains will enable products to better serve local consumers. "We will maintain an open mindset and deepen cooperation with local enterprises," he said.
The European market, including Germany, is among Xiaomi cars' overseas destinations in 2027, and the automaker has already signed memorandums of understanding with eight leading German automotive dealer groups.
Wang Zhisheng, vice-president of the China Chamber of Commerce to the EU, said: "Chinese companies are well aware of the importance of localization — moving from selling cars to Europe to building cars in Europe. We are creating abundant job opportunities for local communities."
BYD's Hungarian plant is set to begin mass production in the fourth quarter of 2026.
Liu Jincheng, founder and chairman of EVE Energy, a major Chinese lithium battery maker, said reaching consensus and co-construction are key aspects of Chinese companies going global.
EVE Energy has built a lithium battery plant in Malaysia and begun nickel resource operations in Indonesia, with nickel already in use in large quantities in luxury cars such as BMW. Its full-industry-chain project in Indonesia will bring electricity to more islands and villages, Liu said.
Li Jiaying, an associate research fellow at Renmin University of China's Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies, said China's real economy is not a source of crisis, but a pillar of global stability.
Describing the so-called "China Shock 2.0" as a deliberately crafted political narrative, Li said that it represents a self-preservation strategy adopted by certain countries confronting industrial disadvantages and domestic deindustrialization. Such countries employ public opinion smears and trade barriers to divert attention from their internal pressures.
Jostein Hauge, a political economist at the University of Cambridge, said the "China Shock 2.0" narrative is steeped in double standards and hegemonic anxiety, while intentionally understating the vast benefits that China's integration into the global economy has delivered to the world.

articles.content_orig:
MONDAY PUZZLE — As Wordplay columnists, we don’t often share our feelings with the solving community. We don’t want to come on too strong, lest it scare off the newer faces. But there are three little words I haven’t said here in a while, and I need the new solvers to hear them: Start with Mondays.
Don’t worry. You don’t have to say it back. This is just a one-way tip for developing a solving habit without tearing your hair out. Monday puzzles tend to be the easiest of the week; the grids and clues get harder as the days go on. This doesn’t mean you won’t run into a few sticking points or have to look something up, but that’s why this column exists.
And who says you have to solve alone? You can always pull in a more experienced friend to show you how to approach a clue list or what to do when stuck. In fact, considering the theme of this crossword by Dena Verkuil, I might insist you make it a double.
The revealer at 59-Across asks for [Words from a bartender … or a hint to the ends of 16-, 26- and 48-Across]. “What’ll it be?” and “Why the long face?” come to mind.
Here’s what we get from the cited entries: The [1989 buddy cop comedy starring Tom Hanks alongside Beasley the Dog] at 16A is “TURNER AND HOOCH.” At 26A, the [Elusive ingredient for success] is SECRET SAUCE. And the [Titular role played by Michael Keaton in 1988 and 2024] at 48A is BEETLEJUICE. Hooch, sauce and juice are slang terms for noxious substances. So, go ahead, PICK YOUR POISON.
6A. Crossword clues often give idiomatic context to their entries. One tends to refer to [Societal woes], for instance, as ILLS. Societal “problems” or “evils” just doesn’t have the same ring to it.

articles.title_orig: Burnham to tell MPs 'landmark' EU deal could make next decade 'much better'
articles.title_zh: Burnham to tell MPs 'landmark' EU deal could make next decade 'much better'
articles.content_orig:
The prime minister will tell Parliament on Monday the "landmark" deal struck with the EU means there is a "very real prospect" the next decade can be "much better" than the last one.
The deal is a "choice between a broken status quo or change", Andy Burnham will tell MPs.
He will also call it "the single biggest growth measure to be delivered in this parliament" - repeating his claim it could add £17bn to the British economy.
The PM described it on Friday as a "win-win" deal with the EU on British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme. But since then a host of politicians have criticised the plan, with one former prime minister urging him to "move on" from Brexit.
Burnham believes the agreement reached in Brussels "holds out the very real prospect that the next decade can be a much better one for Britain than the one we have just lived through".
"The ability to draw a line on a decade of drift and division is in our hands and I believe we should take it," he will say in his speech.
He will also paint the move as a choice "between easing pressure on the cost of living or allowing food prices to rise further" and "creating opportunities for young people or denying them".
He believes polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".
But his announcement on Friday was greeted with a chorus of criticism from a number of opposing political figures.
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal was unfair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels.
She questioned the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".
Badenoch accused him of having "plucked that figure out of the air" before saying "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".
Meanwhile Reform UK leader Farage called the deal a "very good day for the EU", before adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."
Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added in a social media post: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."
Over the weekend former prime ministers including Theresa May, Sir Tony Blair and Rishi Sunak also criticised the EU-UK deal.
May, who presided over three years of Brexit negotiations during her premiership, said she was "aghast" by the deal and warned Andy Burnham should "move on".
Sir Tony, who was a prominent opponent of leaving the EU, told The Sunday Times Britain should only rejoin the EU if it reforms, and allows more innovation on technology.
Badenoch will use her speech at the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) annual conference on Monday to criticise Burnham's EU deal.
She will accuse the prime minister of securing a "terrible" deal and will say he should be "aiming a lot higher" in terms of driving growth.
Farage will tell the same conference that establishing closer ties with the EU would be a "disaster" for British businesses.
Rejoining the EU will hit the small firms that do not even trade with Europe with more red tape, more compliance costs, more Brussels rules they never asked for, he is expected to say.
On Friday, the PM said that over the coming months both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at the options for the UK's "long-term relationship" with the EU.
He was also clear that the deal he struck was "probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it".
He added: "But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."

articles.title_orig: Equipment outage in Atlanta causes over 1,600 Delta flight delays - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Equipment outage in Atlanta causes over 1,600 Delta flight delays - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
The delays were not the result of a systems hack, Delta said.
More than 1,600 Delta Air Lines flights nationwide were delayed on Sunday due to a technical issue causing an outage to one of the airline's weight and balance systems, according to Delta.
The equipment snafu comes as millions of people prepare to travel this week for the Thanksgiving holiday, and just days after the Federal Aviation Administration issued the second nationwide ground stop since the 9/11 terrorist attacks due to an equipment installation problem that caused telecommunications issues.
"These delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems," the FAA said on Sunday about Delta's flight delays.
Delta said later Sunday afternoon that the weight and balance systems had returned to normal operation, and that the outage was not the result of a computer hack.
"Delta is rebooking customers to the next best itinerary and providing meals and hotel rooms where necessary," the airline said. "For customers facing a canceled flight and don’t wish to travel, refunds are being given."
Some 49% of all Delta flights Sunday were delayed by more than 15 minutes, Delta said, after the airline experienced an outage in a system used to calculate the weight and balance of departing flights, Delta said.
The majority of the delayed flights were at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, but the equipment issue also affected flights to Atlanta from other airports, Delta said.
"Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation. We thank our customers for their patience and our people for their professionalism," Delta said in a statement earlier Sunday.

articles.title_orig: Russian vessel hit by suspected Ukrainian drone at Libya’s Benghazi port
articles.title_zh: Russian vessel hit by suspected Ukrainian drone at Libya’s Benghazi port
articles.content_orig:
A suspected sea drone attack has hit a Russian vessel in eastern Libya, causing an explosion and a brief fire, according to the North African country’s eastern-based government.
Local sources told Al Jazeera late on Sunday that an unknown number of Libyan and Russian nationals were killed in the attack at dawn, adding that the ship was moored inside the civil sea port of Benghazi, close to a naval base.
The sources said the ship was carrying weapons, ammunition and drones in its cargo. Local sources quoted residents as saying they saw three drones attack the vessel.
Satellite imagery provider Vantor said imagery showed the vessel was the Merkury, a Russian Navy corvette, or small warship.
Imagery taken on Sunday showed that most of the vessel ‌had capsized and sunk, with only its bow still visible above water. Smoke was also visible rising from part of the ship’s superstructure, with significant debris scattered along the pier.
The Benghazi-based administration earlier said the vessel had docked to refuel and take on supplies under a cooperation agreement between Russia and Libya’s eastern government.
Late on Sunday, the Associated Press news agency quoted unnamed sources as saying that several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya.
Also on Sunday evening, a sea drone hit a Malta-flagged commercial vessel off the port of Benghazi in a separate attack. The Benghazi-based administration’s Health Ministry said all crew members “who were injured when a merchant vessel was targeted this evening by explosives-laden sea drones off the coast of Benghazi” had been rescued and were receiving treatment.
No further details were given. The Almasar satellite television channel said that naval and air forces destroyed at least 12 other sea drones off the Mediterranean city.
The Benghazi-based administration said it has launched a joint investigation with Russia to “uncover the circumstances of the attack, its source, and the party behind it”.
The government said the fire had been brought under control and the site secured, while it condemned the suspected strike as a violation of Libya’s sovereignty and a threat to maritime safety.
“The Libyan government will not allow Libyan ports, territory or territorial waters to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said, adding that Libya was “not a party to the Russian-Ukrainian war”.
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Ukrainian forces have repeatedly used naval drones and missiles to target Russian warships and naval facilities in the Black Sea.
On Saturday, a drone struck a Russian cargo ship in the eastern Baltic Sea near Finnish waters. Finland’s border guard attributed the strike to Ukraine.
A Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast in March after an attack that Russian President Vladimir Putin blamed on Ukraine. Last December, Ukraine said it had used aerial drones to strike a Russian-linked oil tanker in the Mediterranean.
Tallha Abdulrazaq, a Middle East security and defence expert, told Al Jazeera that Ukrainian intelligence services were most likely behind the attack on the Libyan port.
“There was a lot of reporting on the tail end of last year about there being a deal between the Ukrainian intelligence services and the Tripolitan government to establish a Ukrainian military and intelligence presence there,” Abdulrazaq said.
“In exchange, the Tripoli government would get Ukrainian military expertise,” he added.
Libya has been divided since a NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime leader Muammar Gaddafi in 2011. He was killed later that year.
A United Nations-recognised government is based in Tripoli, and a rival administration in the east is based in Benghazi.
The strike in Libya is a “spillover” of Russia’s war on Ukraine and is the “latest example of what [Ukrainian] President [Volodymyr] Zelenskyy has long described as ‘Ukrainian long-range sanctions against Russia’”, Abdulrazaq said.
The prime minister of the eastern-based Libyan government, Osama Hammad, said his government had submitted a formal request to the UN General Assembly and Security Council for an international investigation into the attacks.
Hammad ⁠called for an investigation into “suspicions that the boats had been launched from western Libya… and for verification ⁠of the presence of Ukrainian experts in the country, as well as formal explanations from Kyiv about their activities”.
Libya, an oil-rich nation, remains a focal point for a long-running rivalry between Russia and the West.

articles.title_orig: Russell Brand’s wife vows to abide by prison rules after video controversy
articles.title_zh: Russell Brand’s wife vows to abide by prison rules after video controversy
articles.content_orig:
Laura Brand says in new video on YouTube she will continue Sunday Service series she started with Brand
Russell Brand’s wife, Laura, has promised to “absolutely honour” rules set by the prison where her convicted sex offender husband is being held, in another YouTube video published on Sunday.
This week Andy Burnham called on Google to take down a video uploaded to Russell Brand’s YouTube channel last Sunday that contained a statement from the disgraced comedian in prison, where he is serving a 10-and-a-half-year sentence for rape and sexual assaults.
Laura Brand began the latest episode of Sunday Service – described as a Christian series, which the couple started together six months ago – by telling viewers: “Last week’s episode drew considerable amount of attention and now that I understand the parameters set by the brilliant and professional staff at HMP Littlehey, I will absolutely honour that.”
She went on to address scrutiny regarding her continuing to run her husband’s YouTube channel, amid a Ministry of Justice inquiry focusing on whether Brand has broken rules that are supposed to prevent “serious distress” to the victims of crime.
“I am choosing to continue Sunday Service because I really enjoy it,” she said. “It is also a place where I will continue to be proud to be a wife, a mother and a woman defending her family at a time when the media’s image of what kind of a woman I am is under so much scrutiny.”
In the previous episode, the first published since Brand was jailed – after being convicted of one count of rape and three sexual assaults at Southwark crown court on 5 November – Laura Brand read out a message from him protesting that he was not guilty.
The video, titled “The Good Work Continues”, has remained on YouTube despite ministers repeatedly asking for it to be removed.
That video has now accumulated more than 1m views, becoming the best-performing video on Brand’s channel since 18 May, when he interviewed the New Testament scholar Jeremiah Johnston. Prior to that, the last time Brand surpassed 1m views was on 5 December last year, when he published a video conversation he had with the American conservative influencer Candace Owens. Many of his videos in the past year have drawn only between 50,000 and 100,000 views.
On Thursday night, Burnham said he “wouldn’t leap” to changing the law to force social media companies to take down such content. But he added: “I would call on those social media companies to take these interviews down. You know, why are we having to hear from him? We shouldn’t be, and certainly [the victims] shouldn’t be hearing from him.”

articles.title_orig: Tehran threatens to 'break legs' as 'Trump corridor' prepares to launch on Iran's border
articles.title_zh: Tehran threatens to 'break legs' as 'Trump corridor' prepares to launch on Iran's border
articles.content_orig:
Farzin Nadimi explains how the U.S. could target Iran’s remaining land routes — and why sealing them off will be a "mid- to long-term project."
Armenia is set to launch a U.S.-backed transportation and energy project along Iran's northern border Monday, despite warnings from a senior Iranian official that Tehran would "break their legs" if President Donald Trump and his allies crossed the Islamic Republic's "red line."
Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan confirmed that the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) project would launch Monday, advancing the plan to connect mainland Azerbaijan with its Nakhchivan exclave through southern Armenia and establish energy links with Turkey and Azerbaijan, Turkish media reported, citing Interfax.
The project, a centerpiece of a U.S.-brokered peace initiative between Armenia and Azerbaijan, would also expand American economic involvement in the South Caucasus, where Iran has warned against any development it believes could threaten its security or regional influence.
TRUMP'S FIRST IRAN WAR ESCALATION POST-MIDTERM LOSSES SEEKS TO CHOKE OFF TEHRAN’S TRADE
US President Donald Trump (C), Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev (L) and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan display the agreement they signed in the State Dining Room of the White House in Washington, DC on Aug. 8, 2025. US President Donald Trump said Friday that Armenia and Azerbaijan were committed to a permanent peace as he hosted a White House summit with the leaders of the two South Caucasus nations, which have fought for decades. (Photo by Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty Images)
The corridor has also gained strategic significance amid the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, as Tehran seeks to secure its northern trade routes and limit the U.S. security presence near its borders while Washington maintains its naval blockade and Task Force Iron Gate focuses on Iran's borders.
Speaking at the DigiTec 2026 technology conference in Yerevan, Pashinyan said the new TRIPP initiative, also known as the "Trump Corridor," would strengthen Armenia's regional energy connections, according to Interfax .
"Tomorrow we will officially announce the launch of the TRIPP program, and energy and electricity transit will be an important component of it," Pashinyan said during a public discussion on artificial intelligence.
"We will now connect our network to the electricity grids of Türkiye and Azerbaijan," he added.
The announcement followed a warning from Ali Akbar Velayati, a senior foreign policy adviser to Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who accused Armenia of disregarding Tehran's security concerns over the proposed route.
"I told the Armenian ambassador the final word, clearly, that if Trump and his allies want to cross this Iranian red line, we will break their legs," Velayati wrote in a Nov. 5 article published by the Iranian newspaper Ettelaat, according to Iran's Tasnim News Agency .
TRUMP RETALIATES AFTER IRAN ATTACK AS EXPERT WARNS REGIME IS GROWING MORE DANGEROUS
A view from Armenia's southern border reveals the Arax River, with Iran visible across the water on May 2025. This crossing is a vital lifeline for Armenia, facilitating essential trade and energy flows, especially as tensions rise over the proposed Zangezur Corridor. Iran strongly opposes the corridor, fearing it would sever its direct land access to Armenia and diminish its role as a regional transit hub. The corridor, intended to connect Azerbaijan to its Nakhchivan exclave through Armenian territory, has become a flashpoint in regional geopolitics. (Anthony Pizzoferrato/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images)
Velayati also warned that Iran would defend its security interests in the South Caucasus regardless of Russia's involvement, pointing to Tehran's longstanding opposition to the proposed route.
The roughly 26-mile corridor would run through Armenia's southern Syunik province, near the Iranian border, connecting mainland Azerbaijan to Nakhchivan and providing an onward link to Turkey, a NATO member.
The route would include railways, roads, electricity transmission lines and fiber-optic cables, creating trade connections between Central Asia and Europe.
Iran has long opposed proposals for what Azerbaijan calls the "Zangezur Corridor," particularly arrangements that Tehran fears could weaken Armenia's control over the territory, disrupt Iran's access to Armenia or expand the presence of outside powers near its borders.
In August 2025, Velayati had already warned that the corridor could become a "graveyard" for what he called Trump's mercenaries, according to Al Jazeera .
"Such a corridor will turn into a graveyard of the mercenaries of Donald Trump, not a route owned by the U.S. president," Velayati said, according to the outlet.
Velayati also argued that Iran would act to protect the South Caucasus regardless of Moscow's position, while expressing his belief that Russia opposed the corridor on strategic grounds.
NO RETREAT AT HORMUZ — IRAN MUST NOT CONTROL THE WORLD’S ENERGY LIFELINE
Ali Akbar Velayati, a senior foreign policy adviser to Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, accused Armenia of disregarding Tehran's security concerns over the proposed route. (Photo by Rouzbeh Fouladi/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
During a December 2025 meeting with Armenia's ambassador to Tehran, Grigor Hakobyan, Velayati again raised concerns about the proposed route, according to Iran International .
The project emerged from a U.S.-brokered diplomatic initiative aimed at ending decades of conflict between Armenia and Azerbaijan over Nagorno-Karabakh, an internationally recognized part of Azerbaijan that was controlled for years by ethnic Armenian separatists before Azerbaijani forces retook the territory in 2023.
Trump had hosted Pashinyan and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev at the White House in 2025, where the two leaders signed a joint declaration intended to advance peace, normalize relations and reopen regional transportation links.
The declaration established the basis for the TRIPP initiative, giving Washington a central role in developing infrastructure.
Under the implementation framework announced by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Armenian Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan in January, the TRIPP Development Company would oversee development of the infrastructure.
TRUMP MEETS KEY IRAN WAR MEDIATOR AS UAE REVEALS MAJOR OIL EXPORT SURGE DESPITE CONFLICT
Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan confirmed that the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) project would officially launch Nov. 23. (Photo by ANDREW CABALLERO-REYNOLDS/AFP via Getty Images)
The framework calls for a U.S.-controlled entity to hold a 74% ownership stake in the company, with Armenia retaining 26%.
The company would receive development rights for an initial 49-year period , with an option for a further 50-year extension. Under the proposed extension, Armenia's ownership stake would increase to 49%.
Armenian authorities would retain jurisdiction over the territory, including responsibility for customs, immigration, law enforcement and border security.
The framework also provides for private operators to help facilitate trade and transit, while final customs and security decisions would remain with Armenian authorities.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
On Oct. 28, Armenia's parliament ratified the agreement by a vote of 63-32. Armenian President Vahagn Khachaturyan signed the ratification law Nov. 12.
The United States, Armenia and Azerbaijan also announced the launch of trilateral technical planning groups in November to advance the initiative.
Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title_orig: US targets AI chip exports to China, impacting Southeast Asia cloud firms
articles.title_zh: US targets AI chip exports to China, impacting Southeast Asia cloud firms
articles.content_orig:
Trump says he won't allow American companies to build data centres "outside" the US
Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.
"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.
Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.
Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.
"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.
"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."
But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.
"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.
Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.
It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.
Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.
The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.
Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back
Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.
As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.
Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.
"You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.
"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."
Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.
Meta has already broken ground on a data centre , external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.
The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.
In September Google announced a â¬13bn ($15bn: Â£11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.
Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.
Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".
Google has been contacted for comment.

articles.title_orig: I used Gemini to create an Android app that my family uses; they love it
articles.title_zh: I used Gemini to create an Android app that my family uses; they love it
articles.content_orig:
Parth is a technology analyst and writer specializing in the comprehensive review and feature exploration of the Android ecosystem. His work focus on productivity apps and flagship devices, particularly Google Pixel and Samsung mobile hardware and software.
He provides expert guidance on productivity software, system optimization, and the advanced functionalities that allow users to maximize their device's potential. His analyses are crucial resources for readers seeking to master complex operating system features and streamline their digital workflows.
When he is not busy with technical analysis and software evaluation, Parth dedicates his time to watching K-dramas, studying mobile technology trends and the role of artificial intelligence.
I have experimented with plenty of AI coding tools, but most of my projects have been websites, sample dashboards, or apps that I eventually forgot about.
This time, I wanted to build something that would be useful beyond my own desk.
I turned to Gemini in Google Antigravity with a simple idea: create a household inventory where I can organize everything in one place. I called it Home Vault.
Keeping track of expensive purchases, invoices, warranty details, and service history isn't always easy.
I wanted a dedicated app where my family could find all this information without digging through emails, photo galleries, or physical documents.
With that in mind, I prepared a detailed prompt for Gemini in Google Antigravity.
I named the app Home Vault and asked Gemini to build a native Android application using Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, and Material 3.
I wanted a modern dashboard showing the total inventory value, registered products, and upcoming warranty expirations.
I also require separate categories for electronics, kitchen appliances, furniture, and other household essentials.
My prompt included the ability to attach product photos and PDF invoices, add purchase prices, record maintenance history, and receive warranty expiration reminders.
I even requested powerful search and filtering options, dark mode, and a backup-and-restore feature so my family could transfer inventory data between devices.
Most importantly, I instructed Gemini to generate a working APK rather than a web app or a fancy prototype.
I wanted something we could install on our Android phones without going through the Play Store.
After I submitted my detailed prompt, Gemini 3.8 got straight to work. The entire process took about 30 minutes, which was impressive given the number of features I requested.
I opened the APK file on my Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra, and immediately Home Vault looked and felt like a proper native Android app rather than a generic AI prototype.
Gemini adopted a beautiful Material You design with rounded cards, attractive icons, subtle colors, and neatly organized menus.
The dashboard displayed the total value of my household inventory, registered products, and warranty information in a clean layout.
However, a beautiful interface means little if the underlying features don't work.
Thankfully, Home Vault had plenty to offer. I could add household appliances, electronics, and furniture, along with purchase dates, prices, model numbers, and warranty details.
I could also attach product photos and invoices, which made the app much more practical than a basic spreadsheet.
The dedicated warranty section was another highlight. It organized products by warranty status and made it easier to spot upcoming expirations.
Home Vault didn't feel like a collection of disconnected screens. It felt like an app designed around a genuine household need.
After Gemini finished the development process, I had an installable Android app that I could transfer directly to my phone.
I didn't need to rely on Android Studio to test it. Installing Home Vault was straightforward, and seeing it running on my phone felt rewarding.
I also shared the APK with my family members and asked them to try Home Vault on their phones.
They could add household appliances, attach invoices, and organize important purchase details without my assistance.
Their feedback mattered more than any technical benchmark. After all, I wanted to build something useful, not just showcase Gemini's coding skills.
I should clarify one thing: Home Vault isn't available on the Google Play Store, and I don't have any immediate plans to publish it.
This was never meant to be a commercial app or an alternative to established household inventory services.
I built it as a personal experiment to understand how far Gemini and Antigravity have come.
Generating a working APK and testing it with a handful of family members is one thing, but releasing an app publicly is an entirely different responsibility.
I would need to spend more time on security, accessibility, expensive testing, and ongoing maintenance before considering a wider release.
For now, I am perfectly happy keeping Home Vault as a private project.
Home Vault won't replace a professional inventory management service anytime soon, but that was never the point of this experiment.
I wanted to see whether Gemini 3.8 could take a detailed prompt and turn it into a functional Android app without requiring me to write everything from scratch.
And the results speak for themselves. Sometimes, all it takes is a practical problem, a detailed prompt, and a little patience (and a good amount of tokens).
Now, I can't wait to see how Gemini 4 models fair with such complex tasks.

articles.title_orig: U.S. trade chief sees progress in Canada talks, raises China concerns
articles.title_zh: U.S. trade chief sees progress in Canada talks, raises China concerns
articles.content_orig:
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with China's President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit on Nov. 19, 2026.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is placing particular focus on renewing relations with China as he aims to deepen international trade ties and diversify from U.S. reliance amid a three-month-long trade war with the U.S.
When asked what cards Canada holds in its ongoing talks with Washington, Carney, who recently announced a new partnership with the E.U. , pointed to the country's budding relationships elsewhere.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said Wednesday during a remote interview with the New York Times from Shenzhen, China, where he was among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit . "If the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy.” His remarks came in the wake of President Donald Trump's claim that the U.S. holds “all the cards” after trade talks collapsed in August, leading to both sides enforcing heavy retaliatory tariffs .
Carney and Trump had a meeting on the sidelines of APEC, but aside from a commitment to “continue” negotiations and stay in close contact, no progress was made. However, Carney painted his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a much more positive light. Ahead of the summit, Carney and Xi announced a Canada-China trade pact , which provided additional tariff relief on Canadian food and agricultural exports into China, and in return saw Canada agree to extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
Carney, who is promoting a “Canada Strong” platform as he aims to build economic resilience at home, touted the expansion of the trade arrangement with China as something that will deliver “greater certainty and prosperity for all Canadians.” He also praised the negotiation process with China, saying: “They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”
In an eight-day tour that took him from a European summit in Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia, and finally China for the APEC gathering, Carney forged ahead with his plan to diversify Canada's economy away from its dependence on the U.S., which by far remains the country's largest trading partner .
Experts say Canada's progress in deepening its economic relationships with China could challenge Trump's insistence that Washington holds the upper hand in trade negotiations.
“Part of the Trump Administration’s [belief] is that everybody needs the U.S. more than anything else, and therefore the U.S. has maximum leverage,” says Jennifer Hillman, co-director of the Institute of International Economic Law at Georgetown University. “What this is clearly saying is that Canada can afford to be less willing to give the U.S. whatever it asks for [in negotiations], because they have other options.”
China has the world's second-largest economy , behind only the U.S., giving it the potential to become a much larger market for Canadian goods than some of the other countries Carney has sought to deepen relations with.
“China represents a very big market and the potential of a really big trading partner,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University, noting it could be a leverage point in U.S. negotiations. “Doing a deal with a country like China is something that [the U.S.] will care about because of the size of China's economy and its competitive relationship with the U.S.”
Carney's latest push to strengthen trade ties with Beijing forms part of a months-long effort to renew Canada-China relations. In January, he met with Xi to forge what he called a “ new strategic partnership ,” agreeing to allow in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff of 6.1%, rather than the previous 100% levy. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
The move drew criticism from Trump, who said that “China will eat Canada alive, completely devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life.”
While Canada's closer relationship with China could strengthen its hand in negotiations, experts also warn that it could backfire.
Turnbull points to the latest agreement to extend tariff exemptions on Chinese steel and aluminum as a potential source of tension with Washington. “Things like reducing tariffs on select steel and aluminum products coming from China is something that might make the U.S. and not just Donald Trump, but also [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer angry,” she suggests.
Steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs were among the major points of contention when U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down in August, with both sides accusing each other of walking back commitments.
Carney, however, has played down concerns that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is a major issue for Trump.
“In my conversation with the President, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Meanwhile, some Canadian officials have voiced concerns on expanding trade with China.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned Carney on Monday against opening the door for more Chinese-made EV vehicles in Canada, arguing the “government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars.”
Michael Chong, a lawmaker from Canada’s Conservative Party, during a press conference on Wednesday supported maintaining a dialogue with Beijing, but described Carney’s budding strategic partnership with China as a “risky gambit,” citing potential “national security” concerns.
In 2025, Ottawa identified China as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage against Canada alongside other countries such as Russia and Iran. The Canadian government’s own analysis of Canada-China relations also points out that there are "associated risks” in broader trade cooperation in key areas, such as “prevalent and persistent intellectual property theft, and the risk of diversion of sensitive goods and technologies intended for civilian use for military purposes and applications.”
Carney said ahead of his Asia trip that he would raise concerns about foreign interference in his meeting with Xi. "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” he told reporters in Montreal on Nov. 10. Carney added that he would stress the importance Canada places on "the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”
In a press briefing during the APEC summit, Carney emphasized that Canada's trade with China is largely focused on commodities, rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
“We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork. We are exporting halibut,” Carney said , also citing liquefied natural gas and oil. “These are important industries. These are not cutting-edge semi-conductors.”
Experts point out that Canada could pursue deeper cooperation with other international partners in sectors where a closer relationship with China would be more difficult, including defense and advanced technology.
“[Canada] is not going to partner with China on defense, security, AI, and digital technology, things like that would be very difficult. [Carney] would have an impossible time trying to convince Canadians that's what we should be doing,” says Turnbull. “For those things, [Canada] would be putting [its] arms around the European Union.”
In September, the European Union unveiled its vision for Canada to become an “associate member” of the bloc. During an E.U.-Canada summit in Montreal in October, the two sides underscored their commitment to this plan, paving the way for deeper cooperation in areas including A

articles.title_orig: Libya's eastern government suspects drone attack caused explosion on Russian ship
articles.title_zh: Libya's eastern government suspects drone attack caused explosion on Russian ship
articles.content_orig:
No one has claimed responsibility for the strike on the vessel, which had docked on its way back to Russia
A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck in the early hours of Sunday in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel.
The strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette that had stopped to refuel and take on supplies, according to Libyan officials from the country’s eastern government.
Initial reports said several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, triggering the explosion, the officials told the Associated Press.
Satellite imagery showed the Merkury had sunk after the attack, which took place in the Mediterranean, more than 1,000 miles from south Ukraine , marking a notable geographic expansion of the now near five-year war.
Though Ukraine began the war with no navy, it has developed a sea drone capability that threatened Russian warships in the Black Sea. The Russian fleet has been forced to retreat to the eastern port of Novorossiysk because Sevastopol in occupied Crimea had become unsafe.
Hours later, a Russia-linked cargo ship said to be carrying military supplies, the Ascalon, was hit by a sea drone off the coast of Benghazi. Video showed the drone heading directly towards one end of the vessel, again causing a huge explosion.
Libyan naval forces ‌rescued the vessel’s crew, the ‌sources added. The health ministry said some crew members were in stable condition with minor injuries. The number of injured and their nationalities are not known.
Benghazi is controlled by the self-styled Libyan National Army, led by Gen Khalifa Haftar, which controls eastern and southern Libya and has been aligned with Russia.
There was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities, and no immediate claim of responsibility for the strike, but it comes as Ukrainian forces have stepped up their long-range attacks against Russia far beyond the frontlines.
The ‌eastern-based Libyan authority said port and naval base facilities, including warehouses, were safe and that ​normal operations would resume once the fire was brought under control and the site secured.
It condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya’s sovereignty and ⁠a threat to maritime safety, saying it would take ​legal and ​diplomatic measures against ​anyone found responsible.
“The Libyan government will not ​allow Libyan ‌ports, territory or territorial ​waters ​to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.
The specialist website Naval News earlier identified the ship attacked as the Merkury, a Russian corvette – the smallest class of warship, smaller than a frigate – and said it had almost certainly been destroyed.
HI Sutton, a naval analyst, said the attack was probably conducted by sea drones, after a photograph of one emerged apparently taken off the Libyan coast. The drone, he said, “is also likely the type used in the subsequent attack”. Similar-looking drones were involved in the subsequent attack on the Ascalon cargo ship.
If it is confirmed that Ukraine has been able to blow up or seriously damage a Russian warship in Benghazi, it would represent one of its most successful naval strikes during the almost five-year war.
But it also represents a risky extension of the fighting far beyond eastern Europe, in an incident that could affect civilians on another continent and the working of the port.
A small unit of Ukrainian special forces operatives has been based at Misrata, western Libya, and is believed to have coordinated drone attacks on Russian tankers and transport ships in the past year.
Russian ships regularly make use of the port, which has a growing military importance to the Kremlin, to supply Russian mercenary forces in Africa and as a base in the Mediterranean since the country lost its bases in Syria.
Separately, a fire onboard a Russian cargo ship that was ⁠struck by drones in the ⁠Baltic Sea continued to smoulder ​on Sunday, Finland’s border guard said, with emergency services from Finland, Russia and Estonia working together to put out the blaze.
The Finnish military said the strike on the Sparta II ⁠on Saturday was probably carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remained at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated on to a nearby Russian ship. One crew member was slightly ⁠injured.
On Sunday, visible flames had been put out, with operations focusing on cooling down the containers and stabilising the vessel, Finnish authorities said.
The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, had been damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, Finland’s defence forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials. Kyiv has sent waves of military drones towards the Leningrad region on Russia’s north-west coast this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling on to Nato territory.
The risk of ⁠further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, could not be ruled ​out, Ivo Värk, the Estonian navy commander, told the public ​broadcaster ERR on Sunday.
Finland’s military said last ​week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.
