articles.title_orig: Netanyahu’s Likud, Eisenkot’s Yashar end coalition talks without deal
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu’s Likud, Eisenkot’s Yashar end coalition talks without deal
articles.content_orig:
Talks between the parties of caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form a unity government have ended without a deal.
Representatives of Netanyahu’s Likud and Eisenkot’s Yashar parties met in a Herzliya hotel on Sunday, where they remained split on who would lead the next government and whether far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir would be part of it, according to Israel’s Channel 12 broadcaster.
The Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper reported that Likud wanted Ben-Gvir in government, while Yashar insisted on his exclusion.
In a joint statement, the two parties said they had “outlined their positions on a range of substantive issues” and that a “follow-up meeting would be held”, without revealing a date or any further details.
Eisenkot has until December 6 to form a government, with the possibility of a 14-day extension, after the elections in October gave his bloc 48 seats – 13 short of a majority.
Netanyahu has called for a unity government , saying it was the only way that Israel’s security could be guaranteed. Such an arrangement would allow a government to be formed without the inclusion of parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel, which won a record 19 seats.
Channel 12 reported that former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, who leads the Together list, proposed a coalition of Together, Yashar, Likud and Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu, with Eisenkot serving first and Netanyahu succeeding him.
However, Eisenkot has opposed a rotation, and Netanyahu has reportedly insisted on taking the premiership first, while Lieberman has ruled out joining any government that includes Netanyahu altogether.
If unity talks fail, Yashar plans to seek a confidence vote in the Knesset for a minority government before Eisenkot’s mandate expires. It would rely on outside support from the Arab Joint List, led by Yousef Jabareen, and the United Arab List, led by Mansour Abbas.

articles.title_orig: Trump administration approved shipment of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China
articles.title_zh: Trump administration approved shipment of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Friday said he and Chinese leader Xi Jinping discussed their shared affinity for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during their talks in China this week. Earlier in the day, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the ousted leader was not mentioned in separate talks he had with Chinese officials.
"I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, 'Oh, brilliant, brilliant! He's a brilliant man.' He is," Trump said at a White House press conference.
Asked earlier Friday on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" if Huang, a close ally of Trump 's, had come up in "any of your discussions with the Chinese," Bessent said "no," without elaborating.
A senior Trump administration official later said that both Trump's and Bessent's remarks were correct, and that both were addressing their own conversations. The official spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss those conversations.
Trump also reiterated that he would like to see Huang — who was replaced by interim CEO Colette Kress after resigning amid allegations of an extramarital affair with a Chinese spy — be restored as Nvidia's CEO.
"I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," Trump said. "You know, we're a country of second chances, and I'd love to be able to see him. That's a very important company to us, and he put us in a position where we are literally 10 years advanced over other companies."
Nvidia's board is not considering bringing Huang back , a person familiar with the matter told CNBC earlier this week.
The president's comments came amid growing scrutiny of advanced U.S. chips, including those made by Nvidia, ending up in China either legally or by being diverted via third countries.
Both Trump's and Bessent's remarks are potentially an indication that the Trump administration may not focus on cracking down on China's efforts to acquire advanced chips.
Bessent suggested that U.S. policy allowing the sale of Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips to China remains unchanged following the talks in Shenzhen this week.
"We've already agreed that the ... H200s are the threshold level of chips that could be sold to the Chinese, and, you know, that continues as planned," Bessent said.
"I wouldn't anticipate any change in the policy," he added after CNBC's Sara Eisen noted that Nvidia said it had stopped selling H200s to China.
The administration ignoring the subject of Huang's affair with a possible Chinese spy — whose Singapore-based company Megaspeed has been accused of acting as a cutout for Beijing — contrasts with the importance Trump has placed on beating China in the race to artificial intelligence dominance. It could suggest that despite his support for the U.S. AI industry, Trump is less concerned with addressing China's ongoing efforts to acquire U.S. semiconductors.
Trump has also defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick , who has come under fire from multiple directions for reportedly slow-walking export restrictions on Chinese chip sales. "I understand both sides of it," Trump said on Monday when he also said he's like to see Huang back as CEO.
Bessent's appearance on CNBC came after Trump's return from a tour through Asia that saw him meet with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China.
The meeting was historic as the first time the leaders of the three countries had met without other nations' counterparts. But the trilateral summit appeared to yield few deliverables on any number of the most pressing global issues related to the countries, including the Ukraine and Iran wars or the ongoing AI race.
Bessent told CNBC on Friday that there was a "robust discussion" between Trump and Xi on trade policy and AI.
They "agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions," he said, abbreviating the term "super intelligence," Trump's attempted rebrand of AI.
In a CNBC appearance last week, Bessent lamented the "leakage" of U.S.-made AI chips to China and blamed the Commerce Department , led by Lutnick, for slow-walking export controls on suspected Chinese cutouts like Megaspeed.
Multiple Trump administration leaders have long sought to impose export restrictions on Megaspeed, but Commerce "has the pen" and "you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent said in that interview.
On Friday, however, Bessent was much more tight-lipped.
Asked if there is a dispute between him and Lutnick over how aggressively the U.S. should be pursuing Chinese export controls, Bessent said, "I think we're all committed to following President Trump's instructions."
"I think we are going to see that the ... proper chip restrictions are in place, and the remote access has been curtailed," he added. Commerce recently took steps to close one of China's paths to accessing AI processors.
Correction: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent spoke to CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." A previous version of this story misstated the name of the show.
Editor's note: This story and headline have been updated following additional information provided by the Trump administration about the nature of Bessent's and Trump's meetings in China.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI’s chief scientist has thoughts on how to limit AI development
articles.title_zh: OpenAI’s chief scientist has thoughts on how to limit AI development
articles.content_orig:
A new blog post from OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachocki discusses potential limits on AI development, with a focus on a measurement called perplexity.
Slowing AI development became a particularly hot topic after a former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher said the companies were “gambling with our lives,” and even Anthropic’s IPO filing suggested that the technology could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to society.”
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei then published a plan to “pace the frontier,” seemingly endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Among other things, Amodei called for companies to agree to “common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.”
But to establish a speed limit on AI development, you need to agree on how you measure speed. Pachocki’s post — described by Altman as “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while” — suggests perplexity (not to be confused with the company of the same name ) could be that measurement.
In Pachochki’s argument, benchmarks that focus on AI’s “downstream capabilities” have quickly become outdated as the technology advances. But perplexity — which “measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions” — has remained “informative.”
Pachochki’s post includes a chart of how the perplexity of OpenAI’s models has fallen since GPT 3.5.
“GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models,” he wrote. “Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics.”
So in his view, perplexity could provide the basis for “a shared benchmark for general intelligence,” which AI companies could then use to establish “common limits.” With perplexity serving as a standard measurement for AI progress, the companies would commit not to go past a certain threshold “until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone.”

articles.title_orig: This Is Why Even the Strongmen Are Sick of Trump: Historian
articles.title_zh: This Is Why Even the Strongmen Are Sick of Trump: Historian
articles.content_orig:
By clicking â SIGN UP â you agree to our Terms of Use and Privacy Policy .
Dictators around the globe, some of whom President Donald Trump says heâs âfallen in loveâ with, are growing fed up with the president over his chaotic leadership, a historian revealed.
Speaking on The Daily Beast Podcast , author Simon Sebag Montefiore said that Trumpâs relationships with various autocrats are less about genuine personal affection and more about his awe for their immense power over their countries.
He noted that while Trump has still shown affection for autocratic leaders like Russiaâs Vladimir Putin, Chinaâs Xi Jinping, and leaders in Arab countries, it hasnât been completely reciprocated back in his second term.
Photo Illustration by Victoria Sunday/The Daily Beast/Getty Images
âObviously they have some sort of affinity and, we donât know the details of what it is. I suspect itâs less, letâs say, romantic and exciting than many people like to think. By which I mean, I donât think itâs a meeting of the minds. I donât think it has much warmth or passion âat least from Putinâs side,â Montefiore explained.
âI suspect that when the Russians look at Donald Trump, and Iâm sure this is also true of the Chinese, and I know this is true in the Arab worldâ¦ but I think all of them, youâd have thought that theyâd all be thrilled by the election of Trump, and in some ways they are. But the one thing all these people hate really is spreading disorder, because that can also encompass them and overwhelm them,â he continued.
The White House did not immediately respond to the Daily Beastâs request for comment.
Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and U.S. President Donald Trump held a trilateral meeting in China last week.
Montefiore explained to host Joanna Coles that many of these leaders, namely Xi and Putin, are very weary of the disorder and chaos that they have experienced growing up and as young men, so they are uneased by the chaotic leadership style that Trump displays.
âIf I was to put on my hat as an amateur psychologist, I would say that, you know, Trump grew up, you know, admiring powerful people, worshiping powerful people and aspiring to that power,â he explained, adding âhe talked the language of mafia bosses, but, you know, the real mafia bosses are the leaders of autocracies where they really can order people to be whacked when they want.
âSo in some ways, you know, Trumpâs attraction to people like Kim Jong-un and Xi and Putin is that sort of almost boyish admiration for raw power,â he continued.
He added a counterpoint, saying that âon the other hand also, think that they, know, Putin and people like Xi and Putin, and again, the monarchs in the Arab world and dictators in the Arab world are quite alarmed by Putin, quite alarmed by Trump, and they hate unpredictability and they hate erratic decision-making.â
Autocrats like Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman don't like Trump's erratic leadership style.
Jessica Koscielniak/REUTERS
âSo, initially when he came to power, the view in the Arab world was, surprisingly, this man is wild, is extremely pro-Israel,â he continued.
But he said the Arab world realized that this âcould suit us because weâre exhausted with the hypocrisy of American, traditional American leaders who are equally, in some ways, hard to handle.
âAfter all, they say one thing and do another, and this might be easier for us to do business with,â he elaborated.
He went on, âAnd it looked like that in Trump one. In Trump two, I think theyâve walked back that to find Trump a worry and an alarm. And I know that their general attitude is like, they just wanna get through this intact somehow with all the erratic twists and turns.â

articles.title_orig: I stopped talking to my husband and let AI do it instead. He didn’t even notice | Polly Hudson
articles.title_zh: I stopped talking to my husband and let AI do it instead. He didn’t even notice | Polly Hudson
articles.content_orig:
iOS 27 gives the Messages app a variety of welcome upgrades , including one I’ve found myself using a lot: a Smart Reply feature that’s now personalized to the user’s writing style.
When the first wave of Apple Intelligence features were announced in 2024, one that I immediately thought sounded useful was Smart Reply.
The idea behind Smart Reply is simple. Rather than needing to manually type out replies in Messages and Mail, your iPhone can offer prewritten replies you can choose and send with a couple taps.
Great in theory, but the ‘Smart’ part of Smart Reply struggled to materialize in iOS 18.
Fortunately, with a key Apple Intelligence upgrade in iOS 27, the new version of the feature finally lives up to its name. Per Apple :
Smart Reply in Mail and Messages can now draw on a user’s personalized writing style.
Before, Smart Reply would look at the context of a conversation to craft its suggestions. But now, it also aims to match your writing style, punctuation, and tone.
In iOS 18, I almost never used Smart Reply. That’s because despite being fine at suggesting replies that technically worked, those suggestions didn’t sound like me at all.
That’s changed in iOS 27. Smart Reply now consistently impresses me. It no longer offers generic responses that sound like AI wrote them. Instead, its suggestions actually fit with my normal style of communication.
The only drawback is that right now, you’ll only ever see two Smart Reply suggestions. If Apple expanded the feature by letting you scroll horizontally through more options, I suspect I’d use Smart Reply even more.
Have you been using iOS 27’s Smart Reply feature in Messages? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: Ferrari's New 296 Challenge Stradale Is A 670-HP Race Car You Can Drive Home
articles.title_zh: Ferrari's New 296 Challenge Stradale Is A 670-HP Race Car You Can Drive Home
articles.content_orig:
The curtains open, and for a moment, you're completely transfixed. You know right away that you're looking at something special. This car represents a turning point for Ferrari, a significant departure from what came before. It's a genuine race car that's still somehow legal to drive on the street.
"This is a disruption of balance," says one of the people most closely involved in bringing the car to life. It's easy to see what he means. Even standing still, the Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale looks like a car built with one thing in mind: setting lap times.
Ferrari even calls it "the production car with the closest connection to a competition vehicle."
No hybrid system. 670 horsepower. Just 2,932 pounds. And 1,360 pounds of downforce at 155 miles per hour. The car was developed alongside the 296 Challenge Evo , which will compete in Ferrari's one-make racing series starting in 2027. The price? Around $307,000.
Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale
"It's a physical car, fundamentally different to drive. It's not like the 296 Speciale , which is easier and more immediate." Those two sentences tell you almost everything you need to know.
The Speciale is incredibly fast, but it's also approachable. Its electric motor helps with corner exits, drifting, and straight-line acceleration. The Challenge Stradale does away with all of that. There's no hybrid system and no electric motor to fill in the gaps. It's a raw, uncompromising machine with a narrower margin for error, one that relies on aerodynamics to do much of the heavy lifting.
The connection between Ferrari's road cars and its racing program goes back to the company's roots. Enzo Ferrari lived for competition, and in the early days, building road cars was largely a way to fund his racing ambitions. That relationship continues today through the Ferrari Challenge, a customer racing series that has been running since 1993.
It started with the 348, followed by the F355, 360, and every generation since. The 296 Challenge Stradale brings that racing DNA closer to the road than any production Ferrari before it.
Under the hood is the familiar twin-turbocharged 3.0-liter V6 from the 296, with both turbochargers mounted inside the V. The difference is that it now works entirely on its own, producing:
For comparison, the competition-focused 296 Challenge Evo produces 700 hp.
The turbochargers are carried over from the 296 Challenge, as are the thermal barriers. Ferrari focused its development work on boost pressure, variable valve timing, and insulation. The result is a dynamic torque increase of more than 32 percent compared to the 296 GTB. Without an electric motor smoothing things out, throttle response is also much sharper.
The eight-speed dual-clutch transmission has two distinct personalities. Push the car hard, and it switches to the aggressive shifting logic from the 296 Challenge, delivering gear changes in around 170 milliseconds. At lower speeds, it adopts a smoother calibration borrowed from the SF90 XX Stradale. The exhaust note builds all the way to 8,500 rpm, exiting through twin tailpipes derived from the race car.
Performance is predictably serious. The 296 Challenge Stradale hits 60 mph in 2.8 seconds, reaches 124 mph in 7.9 seconds, and tops out at more than 186 mph. Around Ferrari's Fiorano test track, it completes a lap in 1 minute and 18.5 seconds.
The dry weight is just 2,932 pounds with optional equipment, making it 308 pounds lighter than the 296 GTB. That's also the same figure as the 296 Challenge Evo. The result is a power-to-weight ratio of 4.37 pounds per horsepower.
A big part of the weight savings comes from removing the battery and electric motor. Ferrari also fitted a dedicated transmission with a lighter shaft and casing. Then there's the carbon fiber, which appears throughout the car:
For the first time on a production Ferrari, buyers can also request removable seat coverings, leaving parts of the underlying structure exposed.
One figure says a lot about how the Challenge Stradale behaves through corners: body roll is down 68 percent compared to the 296 GTB. Lateral performance improves by 7 percent, while stability increases by 34 percent.
The springs are roughly twice as stiff, requiring an additional spring mounted in series with the main one. It's a setup borrowed directly from the 296 Challenge Evo. The semi-active dampers also get two additional rebound settings, allowing Ferrari to retain at least some compliance when driving on public roads.
The car rides on Pirelli P Zero R tires, with semi-slick P Zero Trofeo RS tires available as an option. Both were specifically developed for the car.
With no regenerative braking system to rely on, stopping power comes entirely from the carbon-ceramic brakes. The front discs measure 15.7 x 1.5 inches, while the rear ones measure 15 x 1.3 inches. Ferrari says the car can stop from 124 mph in just 331 feet.
The traction control system is predictive and calibrated specifically for track driving, marking a first for a road-going Ferrari. It's all managed by the FIVE system, derived from the one used in the F80.
The headline aerodynamic figure is 1,360 pounds of downforce at 155 mph, a 72 percent increase over the 296 GTB. Ferrari achieves this through several carefully designed elements:
At the rear, a fixed wing derived from the 296 Challenge Evo generates 595 pounds of downforce on its own. There's one notable difference, though. Unlike the race car, the wing doesn't use a swan-neck mounting design. Instead, its supports attach from underneath to meet road homologation requirements, particularly those in the United States.
Ferrari's Centro Stile, led by Flavio Manzoni, took the clean design of the 296 and gave it a much more aggressive makeover. A technical insert on the hood, a wing suspended between two bumper-mounted "claws" inspired by the Evo, black metal mesh at the rear, and a double-keel diffuser all serve the same purpose. Here, form follows function.
Buyers looking to make their cars stand out can choose from a dedicated livery, three matte-finish wheel options, and even colored tire inserts through Pirelli's Color Edition program.
The Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale starts at approximately $307,000.

articles.title_orig: It will soon be too late to regulate use of autonomous weapons, warns Red Cross
articles.title_zh: It will soon be too late to regulate use of autonomous weapons, warns Red Cross
articles.content_orig:
Warning about putting ‘genie back in the bottle’ comes as UN conference fails to agree on regulation instrument
The International Committee of the Red Cross and rights groups have warned that it will soon be too late to put the “genie back in the bottle” as the development of autonomous weapons appears to outpace efforts to regulate them.
The stark warning came as more than 120 member states of the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons concluded a week-long conference in Geneva.
Despite mounting pressure, an agreement to discuss an instrument to regulate autonomous weapons over the next two years fell short of the urgent action rights groups said was needed to address the looming threat.
“We’re starting to see artificial intelligence … being fielded in the battlefield and perhaps also already in weapon systems. If we leave this unregulated, it will be much more difficult to put the genie back in the bottle,” said Dr Cordula Droege, the director of international law, movement and partnerships at the ICRC.
Autonomous weapons are military systems that act without human supervision, often through the use of artificial intelligence or other forms of robotics.
As artificial intelligence has grown exponentially in recent years, militaries and manufacturers have created increasingly advanced weapons systems for both offensive and defensive purposes.
These systems include the use of AI in generating target banks , as was done by the Israeli military in Gaza, as well as semi-autonomous drones in the Ukraine-Russia war, which have “last-mile capability”, where AI takes over in the drone’s final approach to its target.
The president of the ICRC, Mirjana Spoljaric Egger, and the UN secretary general, António Guterres, have called for a legally binding instrument with clear prohibitions and restrictions on use of weapons. In particular, the ICRC has called for a ban on the use of autonomous weapons against personnel, as well as ensuring that weapons systems behave predictably and placing limits on weapons including restricting their use to military objectives.
Experts have said that given the rapid development of autonomous weapons and AI, the failure to create adequate regulations could have dangerous repercussions.
“It’s not about banning all autonomous weapon systems, but to set limits in an international treaty of red lines that should never be crossed,” said Droege. “We’re very close to crossing those red lines, particularly targeting human beings through machines should be a moral red line.”
Other rights groups warned that any delay towards regulation of these weapons risked allowing private industry and militaries to set the norms of how autonomous weapons are used.
Already, autonomous weapons have led to civilian harm. Three civilians were killed by a Russian drone guided by an AI system in July in Zaporizhzhia in south-eastern Ukraine. The drone tried to hit a petrol station, probably its intended target, but instead crashed into a wall, killing three people in a fountain of shrapnel.
In Gaza, Israel has used AI-assisted targeting methods to fill its target banks much faster than humanly possible since the start of the war. As a result, rights groups have said that civilians and people with tenuous links to militant groups were erroneously killed.
In Iran, a US strike that hit an elementary school, killing 156 civilians including 120 schoolchildren, reportedly was a result of faulty intelligence gathered by AI systems.
Anna Hehir, the head of military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute, said further delay to a strong treaty could see “more cases of mass civilian harm that we’ve seen over the past 18 months to two years”, warning that some of these mass casualty events could dwarf what has already occurred. She said manufacturers and militaries were trying to develop “swarm” capabilities, where hundreds or thousands of autonomous drones act at the same time.
“This has the potential for high damage, just because of the sheer mass of systems that would be autonomous. All it takes is for one of them to face algorithmic error and then the entire swarm is utilised and led down a path based on that error … particularly if they’re programmed to target humans.”
There is also a risk of proliferation, as non-state groups increasingly use AI to program their weapons systems, as was the case when the Houthi movement in Yemen used Claude to “vibe code” ballistic missiles.
Armed Islamist groups in Africa’s Sahel region have reportedly used AI tools to improve drone ballistics and for operational planning.
“This is the only thing that is important this week. It’s not really the substance of laws. What’s on the agenda here, after 13 years, is the political will finally present to start to get serious about regulation of autonomous weapons systems,” said a senior diplomat with knowledge of the UN discussions.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu rival condemns ‘Jewish terrorism’ after settler attacks on Palestinian villages
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu rival condemns ‘Jewish terrorism’ after settler attacks on Palestinian villages
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of militant Israeli settlers raided communities on Saturday night, setting fire to vehicles and several homes
Arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank have caused a political row in Israel, drawing condemnation from Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition leader, who described them as “Jewish terrorism”.
Dozens of settlers raided Palestinian communities overnight on Saturday, setting fire to about a dozen vehicles and several homes and scrawling racist graffiti. At least four communities were attacked. Israeli police said they had launched an investigation with forensic teams.
Photographs from Kafr Malik , near Ramallah, showed one slogan written in Hebrew that read: “This is the first revenge.” Several vehicles and homes had been set alight in the village.
Images from nearby Deir al-Sudan showed vehicles on fire. Palestinian reports said an agricultural building had been set ablaze in Deir Ballut and cars torched in Deir Abu Mashal.
An ⁠inconclusive election last month stripped Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister, of his majority. Eisenkot has been asked to form a government, though his prospects seem little better.
“Last night’s arson attacks in Judea and Samaria were acts of Jewish terrorism, in every sense of the term,” Eisenkot said, using the biblical name for the West Bank. “Extremist groups that set fire to vehicles and homes are undermining regional stability, putting lives at risk and doing grave damage to Israel’s national security and foreign relations.”
Referring to the far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, he added: “The actions led by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich in the West Bank have brought the area to the brink of unchecked anarchy.”
Eisenkot, who has been given 28 days to form a government by the president, Isaac Herzog, with a possible 14-day extension, urged the government and security establishment to “use every tool at their disposal – including administrative detention and targeted operations by the Shin Bet – to stop the rioters and impose harsh sanctions on them”.
In an unprecedented rebuke on Sunday, several other members of the Israeli parliament criticised Netanyahu over escalating violence by militant settlers against Palestinians.
Yair Lapid, the leader of Yesh Atid, held Netanyahu’s government responsible for encouraging the attacks. “Jewish terrorism is the product of criminal negligence by the Israeli government,” he said on X, adding that ministers were deliberately encouraging the militant settlers’ violence “through their silence”.
Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats party, warned of the possibility of a third intifada and described the West Bank as “on the brink of an explosion”.
“Anyone who wants to prevent a third intifada must replace the current government, which provides cover and support for Jewish terrorism and abandons security,” Golan said on X. “Jewish terrorism harms innocent Palestinians and Israeli army soldiers, and pushes Israel toward unprecedented international isolation.”
Noam Tibon, a retired army major general and Knesset member, gave a similar warning. “If Israel does not eliminate Jewish terrorism in the West Bank, it will destroy Israel,” he wrote.
Netanyahu has not yet responded to the accusations.
Australia announced sanctions on Wednesday against three people and four Israeli entities, including a construction company, over their role in the expansion of illegal settlements and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
A day earlier the UK imposed sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies involved in building illegal settlements in the West Bank, which the UN regards as Palestinian territory under Israeli occupation since 1967.
Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.
On Tuesday, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman was shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli militant settlers in a village near Jericho, where the group has recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes.
Reuters contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: Trump blames $6 trillion stock market slide on Democrats’ midterm wins
articles.title_zh: Trump blames $6 trillion stock market slide on Democrats’ midterm wins
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump claimed that the war with Iran will end "right after" the midterm elections in the U.S.
President Donald Trump said Sunday that Iran has launched more missiles and drones over the past week than at any point in more than a year, adding that U. S. forces shot them down without any damage and as tensions escalate following the U.S. midterm elections.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump also tied the surge in Iranian attacks to the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress amid voter frustration over the war with Iran and rising fuel costs.
"As everyone remembers, I predicted two things concerning the November 3rd Midterm Elections," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
TRUMP RESPONDS AFTER VANCE BLAMES IRAN WAR FOR MIDTERM LOSSES, VP SAYS HIS JOB IS TO SUPPORT PRESIDENT
President Donald Trump said Iran has launched more missiles and drones over the past week than at any point in more than a year, claiming U.S. forces intercepted them all without damage. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)
"One, that if the Democrats win, the Stock Markets would go down, substantially, which they have, and two, that the Islamic Republic of Iran, which has killed 81,000 protestors as of today, will grow more aggressive in their attacks, which has also occurred. "
Trump also said that Iran launched "more drones and missiles over the past week than at any time for over a year," though he said U.S. defenses neutralized the threat.
"Don't worry, they've all been knocked down, and done no damage," Trump said.
"Iranian leaders consider the Democrats weak, ineffective, and Country destroying, but I won't let that happen!" he added.
The remarks also came days after the Senate rejected a war powers resolution in a 48-51 vote on Nov. 19, leaving Trump's military authority intact.
TRUMP WARNS OF NEW STRIKES AGAINST IRAN AFTER NEW YEAR, CALLS NEGOTIATORS ‘PROFESSIONAL TAP DANCERS’
President Donald Trump monitors U.S. military operations in Iran following an Israeli strike in Tehran on Saturday, Feb. 28, 2026. (@WhiteHouse/X)
Speaking to Fox News earlier Sunday, Trump said he is inclined to resume strikes on Iran after the new year if diplomatic talks fail to produce a deal, warning that Iranian vessels testing the U.S. naval blockade would end up "at the bottom of the sea like the rest of the navy."
In his social media post Sunday, Trump accused both Democrats and Iran of trying to keep fuel prices high ahead of the midterm elections and separately questioned the integrity of the vote without providing evidence.
"Both the Dems and Iran fought like hell to keep the Oil price up as long as possible and, since the Election, the Oil price has dropped by a record level," Trump wrote, adding that it was too bad voters "didn't understand this before they pulled the trigger."

"The whole Election was very 'strange,'" he said. "In the end, America will win! "

articles.title_orig: Finance, fossil fuels and the ‘overshoot’: six key takeaways from Cop31
articles.title_zh: Finance, fossil fuels and the ‘overshoot’: six key takeaways from Cop31
articles.content_orig:
The COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, collapsed Sunday as countries failed to agree to an overarching deal after more than two weeks of contentious negotiations. The breaking point was over the very cause of climate change itself: fossil fuels.
The annual UN climate talks, which stretched deep into overtime over the weekend, hold the dubious honor of being the longest COP in history and the first major breakdown since COP15 in Copenhagen in 2009.
Experts criticized the conference as a stunning failure of leadership at a time when the climate crisis is accelerating with increasingly deadly consequences. “This has been the worst ever COP and its collapse needs to be a wake up call for the world,” said Mohamed Adow, director of the energy think tank Power Shift Africa.
How two words could derail the world’s biggest climate conference
At the final meeting intended to approve the so-called Antalya Pact on Sunday, it became clear there would not be the necessary consensus between the more than 190 countries at the talks to adopt the deal. These did not include the US, which, under President Donald Trump, has pulled out of international climate action.
Deep divisions proved impossible to bridge over key issues — most importantly, including language that the world would need to move away from fossil fuels, a phrase that did not end up in the agreement, and increasing financial support for countries already grappling with climate catastrophes.
The European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands and Norway were among those that rejected it. Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s climate minister who is helping lead negotiations for the EU, said the bloc would not endorse a deal “that does not even mention fossil fuels.”
COP31 president Murat Kurum acknowledged support was not there to gavel through the pact. “We have done our utmost,” he said, but “it is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognize that there is no consensus on this document.”
This invisible, super-polluting gas is a climate villain the world is failing to tackle
The talks come at a critical time for the planet. While attention is diverted by geopolitical turbulence — including the Iran war, which has caused the world’s largest energy supply shock — the climate crisis is accelerating.
A sobering recent UN report confirmed the world will overshoot its target of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. On current policies temperatures are expected to rise to a potentially catastrophic 2.8 degrees. The planet is currently at around 1.4 degrees of warming and the impacts have been starkly clear, from catastrophic flooding in Nepal to deadly heat in Europe.
Yet, COP31 laid bare the enormous gap between those seeking ambitious action, often the most climate-vulnerable countries, and the oil-rich nations pushing back.
In common with previous COPs, the biggest sticking point came down to two words: fossil fuels.
At COP28 in Dubai in 2023, countries agreed to an unprecedented call to “transition away from fossil fuels.” Since then, this has neither been repeated nor built upon as oil-producing nations balk at any reference to the driving force of the climate crisis.
200,000 walruses are forced ashore in Alaska as sea ice melts. Now there’s a plan to protect them
The first draft of the COP31 “cover decision” — which sets out the overarching agreement from the conference — was published Monday and called for “the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems.”
But all mentions of fossil fuels were stripped out of every subsequent draft, despite a push by more than 100 countries to keep them in. “You cannot solve a fossil fuel crisis by pretending we don’t need to phase out fossil fuels,” said Harjeet Singh, COP negotiations veteran and founding director of Satat Sampada Climate Foundation.
Countries and climate groups were also concerned by the agreement’s reference to increasing carbon capture technologies, which would allow for a continuation of fossil fuel production provided its carbon pollution is captured before it reaches the atmosphere.
While many scientists say the amount of carbon pollution means this technology will be needed to some extent, it remains expensive, unproven at scale and criticized as a dangerous distraction from climate policies that tackle the root cause of the crisis.
“Relying on carbon capture without phasing down fossil fuels is like trying to quit smoking without putting down the cigarettes,” said Matt Webb, associate director for global clean power diplomacy at E3G, a climate think tank.
Another huge issue of contention was finance. Poorer, climate-vulnerable countries have long called for more money to help them adapt to climate disasters they disproportionately face and yet did little to cause.
Many developing countries expressed deep disappointment that the draft agreement called for effort to at least triple adaptation finance by 2035 but included no baseline and no specific numbers.
“Rich countries refused to put money on the table to help communities prepare for and recover from climate disasters, and handed polluters a free pass instead,” Singh said. “No deal is better than a deal that locks in failure.”
COP31 president of negotiations, Chris Bowen, said the result was very disappointing but there were “a lot of good things” to come out of the talks, including more than 90 countries signing a pledge to ramp up the electrification of their economies.
Still, many experts expressed bitter disappointment at the world’s failure to meet the urgency of the climate crisis.
“Recognition of the dangers of overshoot should have shaken leaders into action, instead COP31 saw a shameful lack of urgency and leadership,” said Mary Robinson, the former president of Ireland and a COP veteran.

articles.title_orig: Officials warn king tides may disrupt Thanksgiving travel across western WA
articles.title_zh: Officials warn king tides may disrupt Thanksgiving travel across western WA
articles.content_orig:
King tides are expected to complicate Thanksgiving travel on state ferries, with sailing cancellations on one route and vehicle restrictions on others over the holiday weekend.
More than 300,000 riders are expected on state vessels from Wednesday, Nov. 25, through Sunday, Nov. 29.  Passengers are urged to plan for busy travel times and prepare for long waits.
At least one round trip on the Port Townsend/Coupeville route is canceled each evening from Sunday, Nov. 22, through Friday, Nov. 27.  Unusually large tidal fluctuations create strong currents near the Coupeville terminal, Washington State Ferries said.
Such currents make it difficult for ferries to maneuver in and out of Keystone Harbor.
Exceptionally low tides will make some ferry loading ramps much steeper than normal, making it difficult for trucks, RVs with low clearance, and vehicles pulling trailers to board without scraping the bottom.
Scheduled restrictions will be in effect on both Vashon Island routes Nov. 22-29. These include the Fauntleroy/Vashon/Southworth and Point Defiance/Tahlequah routes.
Vehicle restrictions might also be necessary on the Edmonds/Kingston, Mukilteo/Clinton, and Seattle/Bainbridge Island routes depending on conditions.
Riders can sign up for travel alerts to be notified if king tides will affect ferry travel.
The busiest sailings for vehicles are expected to be westbound (or onto an island) Wednesday and Thursday, Nov. 25-26, then eastbound on Saturday and Sunday, Nov. 28-29.
Both directions are expected to be busy Friday.
To reduce or eliminate waiting, riders should consider taking an early-morning or late-night sailing or using transit to walk or bike onto the ferry if possible.
On Thanksgiving Day, there will be a few adjustments to daily schedules on the Edmonds/Kingston, Mukilteo/Clinton, and Point Defiance/Tahlequah routes. Find each schedule by route at this link .
The Seattle/Bainbridge Island and Fauntleroy/Vashon/Southworth runs will operate on holiday timetables.

articles.title_orig: Court bans China’s BYD from selling ‘Defender clone’ SUV in EU
articles.title_zh: Court bans China’s BYD from selling ‘Defender clone’ SUV in EU
articles.content_orig:
Reactions to ICJ ruling underline global divisions over court with China raising concerns about judicial overreach
The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, while China has raised concerns of judicial overreach.
Reactions to Thursday’s historic ruling underlined deep international division over the role of the court and similar institutions. The international court of justice (ICJ) had never previously found a state responsible for genocide and the decision could set a precedent for future genocide claims, notably a case against Israel .
The EU hailed a “landmark” judgment from the ICJ, while the UK reaffirmed “full support” for the court and the international legal order. Australia called on Myanmar to comply fully with the judgment and its obligations under international law.
But China, which has offered rare international support for Myanmar’s military rulers since they seized power five years ago, highlighted “issues such as jurisdiction overreach and expanded interpretation”.
“China … believes that such practices are not conducive to the settlement of disputes,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told a news briefing when asked about the ICJ ruling. “The international community should make joint efforts in this direction to avoid complicating this issue.”
Western nations cut ties with the unstable and poor south-east Asian country after the 2021 coup that ousted a civilian-led government.
Myanmar’s presidential spokesperson said on Friday that the ruling was “unfair”, noting the judges’ nine to six vote. The country’s military rulers have denied carrying out a genocide, claiming their actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted insurgent attacks.
“When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” said Khaing Khaing Soe, speaking at a press conference in the capital, Naypyidaw. “So this was not a unanimous decision … I would say it is not fair.”
The US state department said on Thursday that Washington was examining the judgment, while stressing the need to avoid “politicisation” of the ICJ.
Donald Trump’s administration has taken a dim view of international law, vowing to dismantle the international criminal court (ICC), but has yet to question the legitimacy of the ICJ.
The state department reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”, noting that the US was the largest single humanitarian donor to the Rohingya humanitarian crisis response.
In Brussels, the EU said Myanmar must fully implement the ICJ’s ruling “without delay” and that “compliance with ICJ’s decisions is not optional, it is an obligation under international law”.
“The European Union holds the ICJ in the highest regard and remains steadfast in its support for its critical role in the peaceful resolution of disputes and the upholding of the rule of law at international level,” an EU spokesperson said in a statement .
“The Rohingya people have endured immense suffering, including displacement and violence, and their plight must not be forgotten. This landmark ruling underscores the imperative of justice for victims and the necessity of upholding international law.”
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, called the ruling “a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand”.
The UK expelled Myanmar’s defence attache and called for measures to “ensure the court’s ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity”.
The ruling caps a lengthy legal campaign since August 2017 when Myanmar’s military launched what it called a “clearance campaign” in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. Reports rapidly emerged of mass rapes and killings by security forces, as well as the burning of thousands of homes.
Judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.
The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the ICC – which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states – on allegations of crimes against humanity.
The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited .
While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.
Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part”.
About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across the Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.
Judges at the court based in The Hague have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.
South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion. An interim ICJ judgment in 2024 ordered Israel to ensure its forces do not commit acts of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia . Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

articles.title_orig: Stocks are 'on fire sale' as Anthropic IPO fails to calm AI trade jitters
articles.title_zh: Stocks are 'on fire sale' as Anthropic IPO fails to calm AI trade jitters
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Anthropic's ( ANT ) IPO did little to stem the AI trade's meltdown this week, as the Nasdaq erased its year-to-date gains, leaving it roughly 18% off its October all-time high.
The biggest winners of the artificial intelligence boom are down double-digit percentages for the week, and even more so over the past month, as seen on Yahoo Finance's AlphaSpace chart.
Nvidia ( NVDA ) shares are down 42% over the past four weeks, as Jensen Huang's departure as CEO intensified pressure on an already shaky chip sector. Peer AMD ( AMD ) is down roughly 20%. Meanwhile, memory maker Micron ( MU ) has fallen more than 33% over the past month and is down 50% from its June all-time high.
Concerns over tighter data center regulations, restrictions on chip exports to China, and broader financing worries have weighed across the sector.
Although Anthropic's IPO wasn't the clearing event markets had hoped for, some strategists see the debut as a net positive for the AI trade.
"We're finally getting details with respect to what's underneath the curtain" when it comes to the AI developers, Raymond James Investment Management chief market strategist Matt Orton said on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang.
"Hopefully the market will kind of start to calm down and realize that there's a lot of really high-quality companies that are on fire sale right now," he added.
Orton wouldn't compare the meltdown seen in the AI trade to the 2000 dot-com bubble, noting that startups are now staying private longer as they receive the financing they need and that some of the selling may be year-end positioning to protect gains.
"The market is really healthy," Orton said.
Nomura's Charlie McElligott points out that in recent sessions investors have been broadly selling rather than just rotating into defensive sectors. Instead of "buying the dip," money is moving out of equities and into cash and US Treasurys, where prices move inversely with yields. On Friday, the 10-year Treasury ( ^TNX ) yield sank by 14 basis points to 4.91%.
McElligott will be watching this upcoming week, when computer-driven, volatility-targeted funds could step in and buy, testing whether the recent sell-off is just a dip or a sign that investors are heading for the exits.
"IF by early next week we find the Equities tape STILL unable to stabilize and move higher…it's telling me there are larger structural forces at play, that somebody wants OUT," wrote McElligott on Friday.
UBS strategists noted they still expect the S&P 500 to reach new highs in the months ahead. But "the risk-reward is becoming more balanced," David Lefkowitz, UBS head of US equities, wrote on Friday.
The firm recently downgraded US equities from Attractive to Neutral.
Strategists advise reducing tech concentration and moving into intermediate-duration bonds, such as 2- to 10-year maturities, as they can offer strong yields and portfolio protection.

articles.title_orig: I covered myself in sleep trackers to find the very best
articles.title_zh: I covered myself in sleep trackers to find the very best
articles.content_orig:
Get a better night’s sleep with monitoring and guidance from smartwatches, smart rings, smart bands and sleep earbuds
The best sleep masks and best Bluetooth sleep masks
G etting quality sleep is just as crucial as getting enough sleep. And how you feel in the morning only tells part of the story. Smartwatches, smart bands, smart rings and sleep earbuds can all help fill in the details: how long it took you to doze off, how long you spent in deep sleep, how restless you were, your resting heart rate, even if you have night-time breathing difficulties.
Armed with this information, you can learn how your lifestyle affects your sleep. Maybe your after dinner cappuccino triggers a night of tossing and turning, or you’re more restful after evening workouts. As the wise GI Joe once said, knowing is half the battle. And the more you know about your sleep, the better chance you have of improving it.
As a consumer technology journalist for more than two decades, I began wearing fitness trackers in the early 2010s and have since reviewed hundreds of products in the sleep and fitness space. After spending more than 15 years tracking my sleep nightly, I have a deep understanding of how wearables work, which brands and products are reliable and how to best interpret app data.
I wore up to five wearables at a time (two wrist devices, two rings, and earbuds) for at least seven nights each. Every morning, I plotted sleep data into a spreadsheet, including duration, sleep stages (light, REM, deep, awake), along with average sleep heart rate and heart rate variability (HRV) when available.
The Oura Ring 5 served as our benchmark for accuracy, since it is widely considered to be among the most accurate consumer wearables for sleep tracking. A study by the Multidisciplinary Digital Publishing Institute (MDPI), for example, found Oura Ring’s data to be virtually identical to a polysomnogram (PSG) for all sleep stage measurements – that’s the gold standard method they use in sleep labs.
I also evaluated each tracker for design (is it comfortable to wear, especially overnight?), battery life (do I have to charge it frequently?), and the companion app (is it confusing or easy to read?).
Overall, I tested 11 wearables, some of which I spent significant time with before while reviewing them individually. Other wearables I have recently evaluated that I am confident would not make the cut or that have been replaced by newer models are listed as well.
I keep certain products on hand for future comparative reviews. Some products were sent specifically for consideration in this piece and were returned to the manufacturer if requested, except earbuds for hygienic reasons.
Not only is the Oura Ring 5 the sleekest and slimmest smart ring out there, it’s also the most accurate and easiest to live with.
Why we love it: Part gadget, part fashion accessory, the Oura Ring 5 comes in six color options, from traditional black to elegant Deep Rose. The barely-there design is so minimalist you’ll forget you’re even wearing it, yet it accurately captures detailed sleep data, including efficiency, restfulness, latency and timing.
Easy-to-read bar graphs in the app let you know what areas need improvement. Had restless sleep? Maybe you need to refrain from consuming liquids before bed to avoid nightly trips to the bathroom. Do you take too long to fall asleep? Look into softer lighting, cooler temperatures, white noise or less screen time right before bed. I love the “sleep debt” figure that continuously calculates the discrepancy between how much sleep you got v how much you need. It motivated me to make better decisions to close the gap.
If the info from the app isn’t enough, the Oura Advisor AI assistant is like having your own personal (virtual) sleep coach. Ask it questions about your sleep, such as how to improve, or even ideas for a good before-bed snack.
It’s a shame that … You need a $6 monthly subscription to benefit from all the great features of Oura Ring 5. And even though the battery lasts for about six to nine days, some competitors last longer. Plus, it only comes with a wired charging dock – you need to buy the wireless charging case separately.
Finish options: Silver, Brushed Silver, Gold, Deep Rose, Black, Stealth
Battery life: Six to nine days
Subscription: Required for all meaningful data, $6 monthly or $70 annually
This incredibly thin wristband is inexpensive and free of distractions, but also impressively accurate.
Why we love it: With no screen, the Fitbit Air doesn’t bombard you with notifications and data; it just works passively in the background. When you want to know more – about sleep, steps, heart rate – open the app, sync and explore. The sensors sit on the inside of a thin strap that is incredibly comfortable to wear all day and overnight. It comes in fabric or metal mesh, but Google also offers a silicone accessory band.
The Fitbit Air’s data matched the data from our benchmark Oura Ring 5, closer than any of the other device I tested. This includes total sleep, deep sleep, HRV and near-identical heart rate readings throughout the testing period. The only big discrepancy came from awake time, where it deviated from the Oura by about 40 minutes on average. For example, one night, the Oura Ring 5 logged 58 minutes of awake time, while Fitbit Air only counted 16 awake minutes.
It’s a shame that … You need a $10 monthly subscription to Google Health Premium to unlock detailed sleep analysis and an AI coach, but it does provide enough value to justify it. Battery life of seven days is decent, but it’s not as good as other screenless models.
Sizes : One size (130-210mm wrist size for textile/polyurethane), 130-175 or 165-210 mm (silicone)
Finish options: Obsidian, Berry, Lavender, Fog
Material: Recycled polycarbonate and PBT plastics, silicone
Battery life : Up to seven days
Subscription : Google Health Premium, $10 monthly or $100 annually (optional)
The Apple Watch may be best known for flashy apps, fitness tracking and endlessly customizable bands, but it also makes a great sleep tracker.
Why we love it: The newest Apple Watch looks similar to the last few generations, but it now comes in ceramic, titanium or scratch-resistant aluminum, along with new finishes, including the lovely Dark Bronze of my review sample. I found it comfortable to wear overnight, and the data is easy to read from the watch face and the Health app.
After many years of wearing different Apple Watch models, I have noticed they often overstate deep sleep and understate awake time. This remains true for the newest model, but it comes pretty close to the Oura in tracking other sleep data, with the smallest differential for sleep duration, stages, sleep heart rate and HRV. It also had the closest REM readings to Oura of any device.
Beneath the basic stats, you can also dive deeper and compare your average sleep for the year to date with the year prior, providing value for longtime Apple Watch wearers. Like only a few peers, the Apple Watch can detect the breathing anomalies that align with sleep apnea. It’s not an official test – but it provides enough info to help you decide whether to consult a medical professional.
Besides tracking sleep, the Apple Watch is also a perfect iPhone companion for notifications, fitness tracking, Siri AI voice assistance, and with Apple’s new Health Sensing System, accurate heart-rate tracking.
It’s a shame that … The battery only lasts 24 hours per charge. You also need an iPhone, so Android owners are out of luck.
Finish options: Dark Bronze, Light Gold, Black, Space Grey (aluminum), Radiant Gold, Natural (titanium), Pearl White, Night Blue (ceramic)
Material: Aluminum, titanium, ceramic
Battery life : Up to 24 hours (38 hours in Low Power Mode)
One of the most beautiful Android smartwatches you can buy is also an excellent tool to collect accurate sleep data and get AI-based guidance for adopting better sleep habits.
Why we love it: This comfortable-to-wear

articles.title_orig: Employees at Eric Trump-backed robot startup lose health benefits as company's cash crunch deepens
articles.title_zh: Employees at Eric Trump-backed robot startup lose health benefits as company's cash crunch deepens
articles.content_orig:
Employees at Foundation Future Industries were told that their health benefits through administrator Rippling have been terminated, according to a memo obtained by CNBC, adding to mounting signs of financial distress at the humanoid robot startup advised and backed by Eric Trump .
Foundation told staff in a Friday evening email that they'd be offered coverage through COBRA, the federal law that generally lets workers temporarily keep their health insurance after losing benefits by paying the full premium out of pocket.
"Because our last pay run through Rippling was in October, they have ended our benefits with them retroactive to October," a Foundation human resources manager said in the memo. "COBRA will be offered to all employees to cover November."
Foundation has garnered headlines for the bold claims that co-founder Sankaet Pathak — whose previous startup collapsed in 2024 — has made about his robots and their potential use in war zones. Employees were last paid on Oct. 15, and some inside the company are angry at Pathak for a $4.6 million loan he took from his company last year, CNBC reported earlier this month .
A Foundation spokesman didn't immediately respond to an email or phone call seeking comment.
In the staff memo, Foundation blamed Rippling for the disruption to health coverage. The startup also said it would reimburse COBRA premiums paid by workers and that it was onboarding a new benefits provider.
But employees, especially those whose family members are undergoing treatment for medical ailments, worry the company won't have funds to reimburse workers or reinstate coverage, people with direct knowledge of the situation said.
In a statement to CNBC, Rippling indicated it was Foundation's failure to pay for its employee benefits that led to the change: "If a client enrolled in Rippling's [Professional Employer Organization] is unable to meet their payroll and benefits obligations for multiple months, they will first receive a warning and if not met, they are terminated."
Foundation has been seeking a bridge loan to repay employees after its financial woes began in August. It has been in talks with three or four venture capital firms, including existing investor Tribe Capital, Pathak has told employees, according to people familiar with the situation, who asked to remain unnamed because they were not authorized to speak publicly and feared retaliation. Tribe didn't immediately return a request for comment.
The bridge loan would help the company survive until a possible $150 million investment from South Korean conglomerate Base Group lands as early as December or January, Pathak has told employees, the people said.
Base confirmed to Reuters in recent days that it was considering an investment, but the funding has not been finalized.
The potential investment would deepen business ties between the Trump family and the South Korean conglomerate, an aluminum producer also known for real estate and hospitality projects.
Base paid the Trump Organization $2 million in 2025, according to a New York Times article, drawing scrutiny from Democratic senators over conflict-of-interest concerns. Base has also pursued other business relationships with the Trump Organization, including a Trump-branded golf course in South Korea.
Eric Trump, who has invested in Foundation and was given the title of chief strategy advisor, didn't immediately respond to a CNBC email seeking comment.
The prospect of employees having to pay for their own health coverage comes as many are already drawing down savings to cover living expenses. With another scheduled payday approaching on Nov. 30, workers are facing a third straight pay cycle without income.
Many are actively interviewing for other jobs, and attendance at the company's San Francisco headquarters has fallen sharply, according to people familiar.
Frustration has boiled over into distrust of Pathak's leadership for some employees, while others hope Pathak can secure funding to repay workers and bring the company back to financial health. In conversations and memos, Pathak says that he is highly invested in securing Foundation's future, the people said.
Despite the firm's shaky finances, Foundation continued to hire for open roles until recently and some new workers have never been fully paid, said the people.
To keep employees from leaving before a possible Base Group investment, Pathak has floated the idea of offering workers equity in the startup, the people said.
At the same time, human resources staff have warned workers against taking legal action with California to recover their wages, saying that any employees who file complaints with the state would be dismissed, the people said.
Following a Nov. 14 CNBC report detailing the missed payrolls and a $4.6 million loan Pathak took from the startup in 2025, the chief executive addressed the issue in an all-hands meeting, according to the people.
Pathak defended the arrangement by telling workers that he had plowed his own money into the startup and takes only a nominal salary, the people said.
The co-founder also told employees who were in dire financial straits to contact human resources for help covering personal bills, the people added.
"I'm burning through savings just to afford my apartment," one employee told CNBC. "It's extremely unfortunate we're in this situation."

articles.title_orig: Bessent says we "need answers" on role Nvidia played in sending AI chips to China, suggests Alice Huang is "kind of a canard"
articles.title_zh: Bessent says we "need answers" on role Nvidia played in sending AI chips to China, suggests Alice Huang is "kind of a canard"
articles.content_orig:
Washington — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that the administration needs answers from Nvidia as questions swirl about whether it has complied with export restrictions, after revelations surrounding its CEO's alleged affairs sent the chipmaker into crisis.
"We do need answers," Bessent said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
After Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO amid revelations about extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged spy, the U.S. is investigating how Nvidia may have given China access to advanced AI computer chips, despite government restrictions.
Last week, Bessent referenced a possible "culture of noncompliance" at Nvidia, questioning whether the company was "pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings." In an interview on Fox News, Bessent said he needed answers from Nvidia on its compliance with export restrictions within 10 days. On Sunday, he told Brennan the administration has not yet received those answers.
"We've been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers," Bessent said. "It behooves Nvidia to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was."
Nvidia's CFO, Colette Kress, has taken the helm after Huang's departure. But Bessent has urged the company to bring someone in from the outside to run the company. The treasury secretary said Sunday, "We do need to see who was in charge of compliance there."
Asked how challenging it could be to get to the bottom of what Jensen Huang was doing, given reporting about Nvidia's "handshake" business approach, Bessent said, "For deals that size, there's no such thing as an untraceable handshake deal."
"There are bills ablating that movement, there are money movements," he said. "They may not be the 100-page documents, but it will be possible to understand what has gone on here."
On his call for an inquiry into whether Nvidia had a culture of noncompliance, Bessent said that it's simply a possibility that the dynamic was at play.
"We will see, and that's why I think the board is moving very quickly to establish whether this did or did not exist," Bessent said.
The comments come as President Trump has called for Jensen Huang to return as CEO of Nvidia. Asked whether the president understands the risks that Bessent has pointed to, Bessent replied that it remained to be seen "which level of the business knew about this."
"Was it at the lower levels? Was it at the middle levels? Did it go all the way to the top? And I have confidence that the Nvidia committees are moving very quickly on this and will come up with some very fulsome and robust answers," he said.
When pressed on whether he thinks it would be a good idea for Jensen Huang to return, Bessent said, "I think we have to see where the buck stops — Were these malicious actors down at the bottom of the company who were responsible for the noncompliance?" He also drew a distinction between this possible dynamic, and Jensen Huang's alleged affair with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang .
"I think that is kind of a canard," Bessent said. "Was there a culture of compliance versus one person's foibles?"
Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee and will also be interviewed by House panels in early December.

articles.title_zh: Bessent compares tech outages to vaccines
articles.content_orig:
The following is the transcript of the interview with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 22, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We begin with the Secretary of the Treasury, Scott Bessent. It's good to have you here and in person, sir.
U.S. TREASURY SECRETARY SCOTT BESSENT: Margaret, good to see you.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So there were thousands of customers across America who, when they went to some of the biggest banks, had issues this past week with tech outages, and it caused a bit of a panic with people pulling out cash. In this age of AI, what should Americans be prepared for, and should they worry about their financial institutions?
SEC. BESSENT: It's a good good question, Margaret. And no, they shouldn't. The banks have been at the forefront of cybersecurity for decades. They experience attacks every day, every week, every month, and they are by far the most resilient companies in the U.S. economy. What we are seeing as they, because of the SI, as they go into patch their security systems, the patches may cause a glitch, which is what happened last week. J.P. Morgan went in, and I think the American people should think of it as a vaccine. Your arm may hurt, you may feel a little bad the next day, but it increases your long-term immunity and resiliency.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay. Well, there's other concerns about AI, as you know, and we've seen in the stock market anxiety, a real sell-off over the past week. Nvidia is sometimes referred to as the central bank of AI, since it uses its cash to finance things like data centers and essentially boost demand for its own sales. We have a graphic there, sort of showing the gist of that. I mean, when you look at its size and how interwoven it is in the tech industry. Do you worry that this kind of circular financing means that one company is becoming so hugely important that it could have ripple effects if something goes wrong?
SEC. BESSENT: Well, look, Nvidia is one of our great companies with the management chains. The board has slowed things down. The CFO is now in charge, so you know, I believe that she understands the financing quite well. And no, as Nvidia continues to be fantastically profitable, and there is near unlimited demand for their chips worldwide.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Do you—how do you understand what happened in the markets this past week?
SEC. BESSENT: Well, I think it's a combination of things. You know, we could see that the market sell-off actually began as the Democrats moved ahead in the polls and then accelerated after Election Day. The Democratic position on the SI buildout has spooked a lot of investors in terms of slowing it down. We've also seen some very hawkish remarks from the Federal Reserve. Many people believe that they may be making a policy mistake if they over-tighten. We've seen a substantial tightening in financial conditions over the past few months. So, you know, I think it was a combination of these things.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, President Trump gave that 90-minute or so press conference on Friday, and he did talk about things in AI. Among many things, he said, take a listen to this.
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen, and we're going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.
MARGARET BRENNAN: How is that policy going to work, and won't that also inhibit the sector?
SEC. BESSENT: Well, I haven't spoken to the president about that. I was sitting in that press conference, and I didn't get a chance to speak to him after that. But look, I think the president's very concerned that we don't do a big technology transfer offshore. What we've seen, that the U.S. used to be the leader in the chip industry, and now we see that 97% of the high-end chips are made in Taiwan, which creates a strategic vulnerability.
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's been the case.
SEC. BESSENT: Well, this administration is working to bring them back. There are large fabs being built by TSMC in Arizona, and we hope to have substantial onshoring of the chip business by the end of this administration. So, I think he's worried about the same thing happening with data centers.
MARGARET BRENNAN: With data centers, so one of the arguments against this, and the Wall Street Journal editorial board was pointing out a challenge here, is that if American companies can't build data centers and their AI models close to the markets they're trying to sell into, it will basically give their competitors, the Chinese, an edge.
SEC. BESSENT: Well, look, I think that the SI is very fungible. That companies access U.S. centers. There are many centers in Southeast Asia. They get access from around the world. So I think the real thing here is going to be, and I've said it many times before the election. The industry has done a terrible job of explaining themselves to the American people, and I think they need to have a conversation with the American people, with the communities where these centers are built, and rebuild public trust. And I think once we see that, then we could see a more substantial build out here in the U.S.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, so what the president announced was not reversing, for example, what the U.S. was encouraging in the United Arab Emirates with these data centers being built in some of our Gulf allies.
SEC. BESSENT: No, he's talking about American companies doing it.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, let me ask you about Nvidia in particular and what's been happening in terms of the ongoing revelations. Multiple congressional committees, federal prosecutors, and presumably regulators here in the United States are probing the role Nvidia played in sending advanced AI computer chips to China. On Fox last Sunday, I watched your interview. It was pretty extraordinary. You did not parse words. You referred to a culture of non-compliance at Nvidia. The possibility that they were quote "pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings." You said you needed answers to what was going on within 10 days. That was seven days ago. Have you gotten the answers you need?
SEC. BESSENT: We don't, Margaret. And I think the important word there is possibility. And we have seen. We've been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers, and we do need answers. And back to your question about the centrality of Nvidia to the SI system, it behooves Nvidia to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was. Was there promiscuous attitude toward this, and where—if it happened—where were the faults, and then they can move on.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So when you say we, you mean to Treasury? You're expecting those answers to go to Treasury, or they're expecting to go to the White House?
SEC. BESSENT: To the administration.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Because there was a lot of reporting that Nvidia's business deals were often based on handshakes. That doesn't leave a lot of a paper trail. How challenging is this for regulators to get to the bottom of what the CEO was doing? I know you said the CFO is at the helm, but last Sunday you said basically they need to clean up shop and get someone from the outside to run the place.
SEC. BESSENT: Well, what I said was we do need to see who was in charge of compliance there. Normally, it's the legal department, the general counsel's office. So we'll see what they have to say. But you know, in terms of handshake deals, for deals that size, there's no such thing as an untraceable handshake deal, there are bills blading that movement. There are money movements, so you know, they may not be the 100-page documents, but there, it will be possible to understand what has gone on here.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I mean, that's an extraordinary charge though, a culture of non-compliance.
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's not just the foibles of one man.
